Chapter 2 — Equipment Overview
2.1 System Architecture
The PrecisionBeam IMP-HE2000 is a high-energy, medium-current ion implanter designed specifically for 300 mm
silicon wafer processing in modern semiconductor fabs. The system consists of seven primary hardware subsystems:
the Ion Source, the Beamline, the End Station, the Wafer Handler, the Vacuum System, the High-Voltage System, and
the central Control System. All subsystems interface directly with the equipment controller, which hosts the
SECS/GEM software stack and manages the factory automation link over HSMS-SS.
2.2 Ion Source Subsystem
The ion source is a Freeman-type hot cathode source designed for high plasma stability. Precursor gases (BFI, PHI,
AsHI, or Ar for setup) are introduced into the arc chamber via mass flow controllers. A tungsten filament is heated to
thermionic emission temperatures, and an electrical discharge (arc voltage) ignites a dense plasma inside the
chamber. An extraction electrode assembly pulls positive ions from the plasma aperture, forming a preliminary ion
beam. Real-time parameters include arc current, filament current, extraction voltage, and source gas pressure. The
filament and arc chamber have finite lifetimes and require periodic maintenance, tracked by local timers.
2.3 Beamline Subsystem
The beamline collimates, refines, and accelerates the extracted ion beam. An analyzer magnet acts as a mass
spectrometer, bending the ion path through a 90-degree arc. Since mass deflection is proportional to charge, only the
desired dopant species (e.g., Boron-11) passes through the resolving aperture, filtering out contaminants and
unwanted carrier species. The filtered beam is then accelerated or decelerated in the high-voltage column to match
recipe requirements. Electrostatic scan plates deflect the beam at high frequencies to create a uniform scanning
ribbon beam. Multi-point Faraday cups measure the beam current to ensure stability and parallelism.
2.4 End Station Subsystem
The end station houses the process chamber where wafers undergo ion implantation under high vacuum. A wafer is
held on an electrostatic chuck (platen) that provides Helium backside cooling to maintain wafer temperature below
critical photoresist degradation levels (typically < 120°C). The platen tilt and twist mechanisms position the wafer
relative to the incoming beam, avoiding crystal channeling. A Faraday cup array behind the platen measures the
actual dose in real-time, halting the implant when the target dose is achieved.
2.5 Wafer Handling Subsystem
The wafer handler manages wafer transfer between atmospheric and vacuum environments. It features two FOUP
load ports, an atmospheric transfer robot with a slot-mapping sensor, an optical notch pre-aligner, a vacuum load lock
chamber, and a vacuum transfer arm. Wafers are transferred individually to the process platen, maintaining high
vacuum in the process chamber during lot processing.
2.6 Vacuum System
High-vacuum integrity is vital to prevent ion beam scattering and wafer contamination. The beamline is evacuated by
dual turbomolecular pumps backed by dry scroll pumps. The end station process chamber uses a cryogenic pump for
ultra-high vacuum (~10II Torr). Gate valves isolate the subsystems, and vacuum gauges continuously monitor
pressures across all chambers.
2.7 High-Voltage System
The high-voltage system provides acceleration potentials up to 200 kV inside an insulated terminal. Terminal voltage,
extraction voltage, and suppression power supplies are managed by a dedicated HV controller. Hardwired interlocks
disable high-voltage generation if vacuum thresholds are violated or access panel switches are tripped.
2.8 Safety Systems and Interlocks

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 7
Personnel and equipment safety are maintained through a distributed interlock system. The interlock loop monitors
toxic gas detectors (for Arsine and Phosphine leaks), radiation levels (X-ray monitoring near the high-voltage column),
vacuum pressures, cooling water flow, and the Emergency Master Off (EMO) buttons. If any safety threshold is
exceeded, the beam shutter is immediately closed, and high voltage is tripped.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 8
Chapter 3 — Communication Configuration
3.1 HSMS Communication Parameters
The HSMS interface on the IMP-HE2000 operates in Passive mode, meaning the tool listens for an incoming
connection from the factory host. The default TCP port is 5020. Standard timeout parameters (T3, T5, T6, T7, and T8)
are set to SEMI E37 defaults. These values can be modified locally on the tool's engineering panel or remotely via
SECS-II messages.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'HSMS Parameters', for the complete list of network
settings, IP addresses, port configuration, and timeout limits.
3.2 Device Configuration and VID Ranges
The IMP-HE2000 is represented as a single logical SECS-II device with DeviceID = 1. To organize the large number of
variables, events, and alarms, VIDs are partitioned into distinct ranges based on subsystem and variable type. For
instance, Global System Variables occupy VIDs 1000–1049, Ion Source Variables occupy 1050–1099, and Data
Variables are assigned to the 2000+ range.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'VID Range Map', for the complete partitioning table and
subsystem allocations.
3.3 Tool Identity Block
The tool maintains static hardware and firmware configuration details in its non-volatile memory. This identity block
contains parameters such as the unique Tool ID, serial number, firmware revision, and physical limits (e.g., energy
and current range). These parameters can be queried by the host during initial online handshaking.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Tool Identity', for the detailed equipment metadata and
version strings.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 9
Chapter 4 — Status Variables (SV) — Description
Status Variables (SVs) represent continuously updated, real-time parameters monitored by the IMP-HE2000 control
computer. The host can poll these variables at any time using S1F3/F4 messages or include them in periodic trace
definitions (S2F23) or linked event reports (S2F35).
4.1 Global System Variables
Global variables track tool-wide states, GEM control states, and system-wide safety interlocks. These variables help
the host verify the current operating mode (e.g., IDLE, IMPLANTING) and ensure safety conditions are met before
starting a run.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Global System', for the complete list of global
variables, including SystemStatus, ControlState, and EMOStatus.
4.2 Ion Source Variables
Ion source variables monitor the health and discharge characteristics of the Freeman plasma source. Parameters
include arc current, filament current, filament voltage, extraction voltage, gas flow rate, and gas species. These values
are refreshed every 500 ms.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Ion Source', for all source-related SVs.
4.3 Beamline Variables
Beamline variables monitor ion beam transport and beam qualities, such as mass analyzer coil current, beam energy,
resolved Faraday cup current, electrostatic scan frequencies, spot sizes, and beam parallelism. These are critical to
verify that the ion beam is properly tuned and aligned before implanting the wafer.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Beamline', for the beamline variables list.
4.4 End Station Variables
End station variables track process chamber parameters during implantation, including platen tilt/twist angles, wafer
clamp status, backside helium cooling flow, and real-time dose accumulation. Fast updates (200 ms) are provided for
critical dose and beam current parameters.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - End Station', for end station SV details.
4.5 Wafer Handler Variables
Wafer handler variables track the robot state, robot end-effector positions, load lock chamber pressure, load lock
pump/vent states, pre-aligner notch angle, and FOUP wafer mapping counts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Wafer Handler', for handling SVs.
4.6 Vacuum System Variables
Vacuum system variables monitor pressures in the beamline, process chamber, and source chamber, as well as
turbomolecular pump speeds, cryopump cold-head temperature, and isolation gate valve positions.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Vacuum System', for vacuum SVs.
4.7 High-Voltage and Power Variables
High-voltage variables monitor terminal acceleration voltage, suppression voltage, extraction voltage, and power
supply status. Host software should verify that terminal voltage matches recipe targets prior to beam-on commands.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 10
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - High Voltage and Power', for high-voltage and power
status variables.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies

Chapter 5 — Data Variables (DV) — Description
Data Variables (DVs) differ from Status Variables in that their values are event-dependent. They represent process
setup targets and post-process results (such as lot ID, recipe settings, measured dose, uniformity, and particle
counts). These values are updated at specific event triggers (like ImplantStart and ImplantEnd) and are typically read
by the host inside linked reports rather than polled during idle periods.
5.1 Recipe and Implant Target Variables
These variables capture the target process parameters defined in the active recipe, including the Target Species,
Target Energy, Target Dose, and Target Platen Tilt/Twist angles. They are updated when a recipe is loaded or an
implant run starts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Recipe and Implant Targets', for recipe DVs.
5.2 Process Result and Metrology Variables
Post-process variables contain metrology and quality assurance results for the most recently processed wafer, such
as actual dose delivered, measured dose uniformity, average beam current, implant duration, maximum wafer
temperature, ellipsometry results, and the process outcome (PASS/FAIL). These variables are updated when the
wafer processing ends or is aborted.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Process Results', for results and metrology DVs.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 12
Chapter 6 — Collection Events (CEID) — Description
Collection Events (CEIDs) represent milestones in the equipment's physical and logical workflow. When an event
occurs, the equipment sends an S6F11 Event Report message containing linked reports to the host. The host can
dynamically enable or disable reporting for individual event IDs using the S2F37 message.
6.1 Implant Lifecycle Events
Implant lifecycle events track progress during wafer processing. The primary lifecycle events are ImplantStart,
ImplantEnd, and ImplantAbort. These events allow the host to track processing times and receive detailed
post-implant results immediately after a wafer is processed.
6.2 Beam Tuning Events
Beam tuning events notify the host of beam preparation progress. They include BeamTuneStart, BeamTuneComplete,
BeamLost, SourceIgnition, SourceExtinguish, and SourceFault. These events help the host monitor source stability
and track beam setup durations.
6.3 Wafer Handling Events
Handling 
events 
track 
wafer 
and 
FOUP 
movements. 
Key 
events 
include 
WaferLoaded_EndStation,
WaferUnloaded_EndStation, 
WaferPrealigned, 
FOUPLoaded_Port1/2, 
FOUPUnloaded_Port1/2,
LoadLockPumpDown, LoadLockVacuumReached, and LoadLockVent. These events allow tracking of wafer locations
within the tool.
6.4 System and Maintenance Events
System events track state changes and maintenance intervals. They include ControlStateChange, RecipeLoaded,
RecipeDeleted, 
MaintenanceModeEntered/Exited, 
HV_Enabled/Disabled, 
AlarmSet/Cleared, 
and
PMDue_Source/Beamline. These events alert the host to configuration changes and required maintenance actions.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Collection Events', for the complete list of CEIDs, linked
variables, and trigger conditions.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies

Chapter 7 — Reports (RPTID) — Description
Reports (RPTIDs) are host-defined or factory-default structures that group multiple variables. By linking reports to
events, the host receives only the relevant parameters when an event occurs, minimising network traffic and
processing overhead. Report definition is managed via S2F33, and linking is performed via S2F35.
7.1 Standard Linked Reports
The IMP-HE2000 defines 14 standard reports, including RPT_ImplantStart, RPT_ImplantEnd, RPT_BeamStatus,
RPT_WaferLoad, RPT_AlarmEvent, RPT_SourceStatus, and RPT_VacuumStatus. These reports group relevant
status and data variables to provide a complete status update at the moment an event is triggered.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Reports', for details of all default reports and their
variables.
7.2 Report–Event Linking
The equipment controller maintains a default linking configuration to provide standard GEM reports out-of-the-box. For
example, the ImplantStart event is linked to RPT_ImplantStart and RPT_BeamStatus, ensuring the host receives both
process targets and beam parameters at start.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Report-Event Links', for the default links table.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 14
Chapter 8 — Alarm Management — Description
Alarms are generated when an operational parameter exceeds safe limits or a hardware failure is detected. Alarms are
reported to the host immediately via S5F1 messages. In addition, an AlarmSet event is triggered, allowing the host to
receive a linked report with system status details. Host control systems should monitor alarms to interlock factory
automation tasks.
8.1 Critical Alarms
Critical Alarms represent severe faults that cause an immediate process abort, close the beam shutter, and trip high
voltage. Examples include Source_ArcFault, Source_GasLeak, Beam_EnergyContamination, EndStn_DoseOverrun,
HV_ArcOver, Vacuum leaks, and EMO activation.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Critical', for the complete list of critical alarms,
codes, and linked SVIDs.
8.2 Warning Alarms
Warning Alarms notify the operator of degraded performance or upcoming maintenance needs without aborting the
active process. Examples include Source_FilamentDegraded, Beam_CurrentInstability, EndStn_CoolantFlowLow,
cryopump temperature drift, and pending PM counters.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Warning', for all warning alarms.
8.3 Alarm Response Procedures (Detailed)
When an alarm is received by the host, the factory control system should log the Alarm ID and text, check linked
variables (e.g., pressure or temperature SVIDs) to assess severity, and notify the operator. Critical alarms require
manual operator investigation, hardware repair (if needed), and a RESET_FAULT command to clear the error state.
Step-by-step recovery details are provided in Appendix C.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 15
Chapter 9 — Remote Commands (RCMD) — Description
Remote Commands allow the host to control equipment operations using S2F41 messages. Commands can include
parameters (e.g., recipe name, wafer ID) passed as CPNAME/CPVAL pairs. The equipment replies with S2F42
containing the HCACK code indicating acceptance or rejection.
9.1 Process Control Commands
Process control commands manage the implant run. They include START_IMPLANT (starts the run with specified
RECIPE_ID and WAFER_ID parameters), ABORT_IMPLANT (aborts the run immediately), PAUSE_IMPLANT, and
RESUME_IMPLANT. These commands allow full automated operation of wafer lots.
9.2 Beam and Source Commands
These commands manage beam preparation, including TUNE_BEAM (initiates tuning for species and energy
setpoints), SOURCE_ON (ignites source plasma with specified gas), SOURCE_OFF, HV_ON, and HV_OFF. These
allow the host to prepare the tool prior to starting a process lot.
9.3 Maintenance and Configuration Commands
Maintenance commands assist with calibration and troubleshooting. They include LOAD_RECIPE, DELETE_RECIPE,
ENTER_MAINTENANCE, EXIT_MAINTENANCE, RESET_FAULT (clears fault state to IDLE), SET_CLOCK,
RESET_PM_COUNTER, PUMP_DOWN_LOADLOCK, and VENT_LOADLOCK.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Remote Commands', for all command names, parameter
requirements, and resulting events.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 16
Chapter 10 — Equipment State Machine
10.1 State Definitions
The IMP-HE2000 process state machine represents the physical status of the implanter. The primary states are: IDLE
(ready to accept commands), SETTING_UP (recipe loaded, source warming, beam tuning active), BEAM_READY
(beam stable, waiting for wafer), LOADING (transferring wafer to platen), ALIGNING (moving platen to tilt/twist
angles), IMPLANTING (beam on, scanning, dose accumulating), UNLOADING (wafer returning to load lock),
COMPLETED (run finished), FAULT (stopped due to alarm), and MAINTENANCE (servicing active).
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'State Definitions', for definitions of all process states.
10.2 Transition Logic
Transitions occur in response to host commands (manual) or equipment events (automatic). For example, receiving a
START_IMPLANT command triggers a transition from IDLE to SETTING_UP. Once beam tuning completes, the tool
automatically transitions to BEAM_READY. Critical alarms trigger an automatic transition from any active state to
FAULT.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'State Transitions', for the complete transition table,
including source states, destination states, triggers, and manual/auto classifications.
10.3 GEM Control State Overlay
The GEM Control State machine governs the host-equipment relationship. It operates independently of the process
state machine and consists of: OFF-LINE (no host communication), ON-LINE LOCAL (host can read data, but
commands are rejected except for online request), and ON-LINE REMOTE (host has full control, can send remote
commands and recipes). Control state transitions are reported via the ControlStateChange event.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 17
Chapter 11 — SECS-II Message Summary
This chapter summarizes the SECS-II stream and function messages supported by the IMP-HE2000. The supported
messages cover the required GEM capabilities and selected optional capabilities required for factory host integration.
11.1 Host-to-Equipment Messages
Host-to-Equipment messages are sent by the factory host to request status, send commands, manage recipes, or
configure reports. Key streams include S1 (status requests), S2 (configuration/control), S5 (alarm enable), S7 (recipe
transfer), and S10 (terminal display).
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Messages H to E', for the complete summary of
host-initiated messages.
11.2 Equipment-to-Host Messages
Equipment-to-Host messages are sent by the tool to reply to host requests, report events, send trace data, or notify
the host of alarms. Key streams include S1 (status replies), S2 (command acknowledges), S5 (alarm reports), S6
(event reports), and S9 (system errors).
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Messages E to H', for the summary of equipment-initiated
messages.

Appendix A — GEM Compliance Matrix (Prose)
The IMP-HE2000 complies with all mandatory capabilities defined in the SEMI E30 Generic Equipment Model
standard, including Establish Communications, Process Program Management, Equipment Self-Description, Control,
Alarm Management, and Event Notification. It also implements several optional capabilities, such as Variable Data
Collection, Limits Monitoring, enhanced recipe management, equipment terminal services, and clock synchronization.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'GEM Compliance', for the complete compliance matrix
mapping each standard capability to its implementing SECS-II stream/function pairs.

Appendix B — Operational Scenarios (Prose)
B.1 Communication and Configuration Setup
1. Host connection: Host initiates a TCP connection to the tool IP and port 5020. Once established, host sends
S1F13 (Establish Communications).
2. Tool acknowledge: The tool verifies network parameters and replies with S1F14 (COMMACK=0x00). The GEM
Control State transitions to ON-LINE.
3. Report definitions: Host sends S2F33 to define standard reports (e.g., linking report 3101 to variables for beam
and dose). The tool replies with S2F34 (DRACK=0x00).
4. Link reports to events: Host sends S2F35 to link reports to events (e.g., linking event 3001 to report 3101). Tool
replies with S2F36 (LRACK=0x00).
5. Enable event notifications: Host sends S2F37 to enable event notifications for lot tracking. Tool replies with
S2F38 (ERACK=0x00).
B.2 Successful Implant Process Run
1. Recipe upload: Host uploads process recipe 'B_120K_1E15' using S7F3. Tool replies with S7F4 (ACKC7=0x00).
2. 
Implant 
start 
command: 
Host 
sends 
S2F41 
with 
command 
START_IMPLANT 
and 
parameters
RECIPE_ID='B_120K_1E15', WAFER_ID='WFR-B24', SLOT_NUMBER=5. Tool checks safety interlocks and replies
with S2F42 (HCACK=0x00).
3. Tuning and load lock pump: Tool transitions to SETTING_UP state. The source plasma is ignited, and the load
lock pumps down. Once vacuum and beam parameters are ready, tool transitions to BEAM_READY.
4. Wafer loading and alignment: The wafer is loaded onto the platen, and the platen moves to the tilt/twist angles.
The tool sends S6F11 for WaferLoaded_EndStation (CEID 3010).
5. Implant active: The beam shutter opens, and implantation begins. Tool sends S6F11 for ImplantStart (CEID 3001).
6. Dose achieved: When target dose is achieved (1e15 ions/cm²), the beam shutter closes. Tool sends S6F11 for
ImplantEnd (CEID 3002) containing report 3102 with delivered dose, uniformity, and PASS result.
7. Wafer unload: The platen returns to home position, and the robot transfers the wafer back to the FOUP. Tool sends
S6F11 for WaferUnloaded_EndStation (CEID 3011).
B.3 Alarm Interlock Handling
1. Overheat alarm: During active implantation, if wafer temperature exceeds 120°C, the tool ignites a critical alarm
and immediately sends S5F1 (ALID=4006, ALTX='EndStn_WaferOverheat').
2. Process abort: Simultaneously, the beam shutter closes, and the tool transitions to FAULT state. The tool sends
S6F11 for ImplantAbort (CEID 3003) and AlarmSet (CEID 3037).
3. Host investigation: Host receives the alarm, queries SVID 1159 (measured wafer temperature), and logs the error.
4. Recovery: Operator checks backside cooling helium flow and clears platen debris. Once temperature drops below
safe threshold, operator issues a reset command. Host sends S2F41 with command RESET_FAULT. Tool clears the
fault, sends S5F1 (ALCD=0x00, ALID=4006, ALTX='Wafer temperature cleared'), and transitions to IDLE state.

IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual  |  Revision A  |  PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 23
Appendix C — Alarm Recovery Procedures (Detailed Step-by-Step)
ALID 4001 — Source_ArcFault
1. Tool automatically shuts off plasma and closes the beam shutter. High voltage remains disabled.
2. Host receives S5F1 for ALID 4001. Operator should verify SVID 1051 (arc current) and SVID 1052 (arc voltage).
3. Inspect tungsten filament and arc chamber for degradation. Filament operational hours are checked via SVID 1061.
4. If filament is thin or broken, perform source maintenance and reset source lifetime hours counter.
5. After hardware check, send RESET_FAULT RCMD to return to IDLE state.
ALID 4002 — Source_GasLeak
1. Hardwired interlocks close toxic gas cabinet pneumatic valves immediately and trigger facility exhaust alarms.
2. Host receives S5F1 for ALID 4002. Evacuate all personnel from the gas box and tool bay immediately.
3. Notify facility safety officer. Do not attempt local tool reset.
4. Verify leak condition using facility ambient gas monitors.
5. Once cleared, reset facility safety loops, then send RESET_FAULT RCMD from host.
ALID 4005 — EndStn_DoseOverrun
1. Tool closes the electrostatic beam shutter, terminates wafer scanning, and transitions to FAULT.
2. Host receives S5F1 for ALID 4005 and ImplantAbort event report.
3. Check actual dose delivered (DVID 2051) against recipe target (DVID 2008). Check beam stability (DVID 2062).
4. Calibrate dose Faraday cups. Check dose integrator electronics.
5. Send RESET_FAULT RCMD, unload the damaged wafer, and restart process with a test wafer.
ALID 4006 — EndStn_WaferOverheat
1. Beam shutter is closed, platen mechanical scanning is stopped, and tool transitions to FAULT.
2. Check measured wafer temperature (SVID 1159). Monitor until wafer cools down below 50°C.
3. Check backside Helium coolant pressure (SVID 1163) and coolant flow rate (SVID 1162).
4. Verify electrostatic clamp voltage and chuck surface cleanliness. Confirm clamp release works.
5. Once hardware is verified and temperature is below safe threshold, send RESET_FAULT RCMD.

Chapter 1 â Introduction
1.1 Purpose and Scope
This manual describes the operation, architecture, and SECS/GEM host interface of the IMP-HE2000 High-Energy
Medium-Current Ion Implanter manufactured by PrecisionBeam Technologies. It covers equipment subsystems,
process workflows, state machine behaviour, alarm handling, and remote command capabilities. For all tabular data â
including variable IDs, event codes, alarm definitions, report structures, and state transitions â refer to the companion
workbook: IMP_HE2000_Variable_Tables.xlsx.
1.2 How to Use This Manual
This manual is the prose companion to the Variable Tables workbook. The manual explains HOW the equipment
works and WHY variables/events/alarms exist. The workbook provides the WHAT â exact IDs, types, ranges, and
linkages. Together they form the complete SECS/GEM Interface Control Document (ICD).
1.3 Companion Documentshh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$5f75442f-7788-4bd0-a5fe-10d287d5e556h
)}(h
}(hh@h}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhX|␀␀linkages. Together they form the complete SECS/GEM Interface Control Document (ICD).
1.3 Companion Documents
The following companion documents should be read in conjunction with this manual:
â¢ IMP_HE2000_Variable_Tables.xlsx â All variable, event, alarm, report, and command tables.
â¢ IMP-HE2000-GEM-ICD-001 Rev A â Combined engineering specification (future release).
1.4 Terminology and Abbreviations
AMU (Atomic Mass Unit): The unit of measurement used to specify the mass of ions. It is critical in mass
spectrometry and ion beam mass analysis to ensure only the desired dopant species is selected and accelerated
toward the wafer.
AsHI (Arsine): A toxic process gas used as a precursor to supply Arsenic (As) ions for n-type doping of silicon
substrates.
BFI (Boron Trifluoride): A process gas commonly used to supply Boron (B) ions for p-type doping in semiconductor
processing.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$b40b7cbb-d071-41ef-9241-fbb6a1a6ac84h

BFI (Boron Trifluoride): A process gas commonly used to supply Boron (B) ions for p-type doping in semiconductor
processing.
CEID (Collection Event ID): A unique numeric identifier representing an equipment event that the host can subscribe
to, such as a process step starting, wafer loading, or status transition.
DV / DVID (Data Variable / Data Variable ID): A dynamic variable whose value is updated only during or upon
completion of specific events (e.g., post-implant wafer results).
EC (Equipment Constant): A user-configurable setpoint or operational parameter stored in the equipment controller
that governs local tool behaviour and can be modified by the host.
GEM (Generic Equipment Model): The SEMI E30 standard defining a generic model for communications and control
of manufacturing equipment by a host computer in a semiconductor fab.
HSMS (High-Speed Message Services): The SEMI E37 standard defining the TCP/IP-based transport layer protocolhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$ecdf58e4-c561-409f-8f14-2a1b0b835e89h

HSMS (High-Speed Message Services): The SEMI E37 standard defining the TCP/IP-based transport layer protocol
used to transmit SECS-II messages between the equipment and the host.
keV (kilo-electron-Volt): A unit of energy representing the kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerating through a
potential difference of one thousand volts. It is the standard unit for specifying ion beam energy.
MFC (Mass Flow Controller): An active device used to precisely measure and control the flow rate of process gases
into the plasma arc chamber of the ion source.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$46e180e0-f6d5-456c-a1cc-e4cae8e70cceh

PHI (Phosphine): A toxic process gas used to supply Phosphorus (P) ions for n-type doping in silicon wafers.
RCMD (Remote Command): A host-initiated instruction sent to the equipment to trigger a physical or logical change
(e.g., START_IMPLANT, ABORT_IMPLANT).
RPT / RPTID (Report / Report ID): A grouping of status or data variables defined by the host and linked to collection

SECS-II (SEMI Equipment Communications Standard 2): The SEMI E5 standard defining the message structure

VID (Variable ID): A generic term referencing any status variable (SVID) or data variable (DVID).

Chapter 2 â Equipment Overview
2.1 System Architecture
The PrecisionBeam IMP-HE2000 is a high-energy, medium-current ion implanter designed specifically for 300 mm
silicon wafer processing in modern semiconductor fabs. The system consists of seven primary hardware subsystems:
the Ion Source, the Beamline, the End Station, the Wafer Handler, the Vacuum System, the High-Voltage System, and
the central Control System. All subsystems interface directly with the equipment controller, which hosts the
SECS/GEM software stack and manages the factory automation link over HSMS-SS.
2.2 Ion Source Subsystem
The ion source is a Freeman-type hot cathode source designed for high plasma stability. Precursor gases (BFI, PHI,
AsHI, or Ar for setup) are introduced into the arc chamber via mass flow controllers. A tungsten filament is heated tohh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$499cd808-b183-4fcf-8559-53eb8579f113h
)}(h
}(hhjh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhX␀␀AsHI, or Ar for setup) are introduced into the arc chamber via mass flow controllers. A tungsten filament is heated to
thermionic emission temperatures, and an electrical discharge (arc voltage) ignites a dense plasma inside the
chamber. An extraction electrode assembly pulls positive ions from the plasma aperture, forming a preliminary ion
beam. Real-time parameters include arc current, filament current, extraction voltage, and source gas pressure. The
filament and arc chamber have finite lifetimes and require periodic maintenance, tracked by local timers.
2.3 Beamline Subsystem
The beamline collimates, refines, and accelerates the extracted ion beam. An analyzer magnet acts as a mass
spectrometer, bending the ion path through a 90-degree arc. Since mass deflection is proportional to charge, only the
desired dopant species (e.g., Boron-11) passes through the resolving aperture, filtering out contaminants andhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$ff297228-b13b-44fe-905d-dabf9b119b3dh
)}(h
}(hhqh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXå␀␀desired dopant species (e.g., Boron-11) passes through the resolving aperture, filtering out contaminants and
unwanted carrier species. The filtered beam is then accelerated or decelerated in the high-voltage column to match
recipe requirements. Electrostatic scan plates deflect the beam at high frequencies to create a uniform scanning
ribbon beam. Multi-point Faraday cups measure the beam current to ensure stability and parallelism.
2.4 End Station Subsystem
The end station houses the process chamber where wafers undergo ion implantation under high vacuum. A wafer is
held on an electrostatic chuck (platen) that provides Helium backside cooling to maintain wafer temperature below
critical photoresist degradation levels (typically < 120Â°C). The platen tilt and twist mechanisms position the wafer
relative to the incoming beam, avoiding crystal channeling. A Faraday cup array behind the platen measures the
actual dose in real-time, halting the implant when the target dose is achieved.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$3b9a8853-7a5a-463c-a009-c8f80d062ea7h
)}(h
}(hhxh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhK
uhXâ␀␀relative to the incoming beam, avoiding crystal channeling. A Faraday cup array behind the platen measures the
actual dose in real-time, halting the implant when the target dose is achieved.
2.5 Wafer Handling Subsystem
The wafer handler manages wafer transfer between atmospheric and vacuum environments. It features two FOUP
load ports, an atmospheric transfer robot with a slot-mapping sensor, an optical notch pre-aligner, a vacuum load lock
chamber, and a vacuum transfer arm. Wafers are transferred individually to the process platen, maintaining high
vacuum in the process chamber during lot processing.
2.6 Vacuum System
High-vacuum integrity is vital to prevent ion beam scattering and wafer contamination. The beamline is evacuated by
dual turbomolecular pumps backed by dry scroll pumps. The end station process chamber uses a cryogenic pump for
ultra-high vacuum (~10II Torr). Gate valves isolate the subsystems, and vacuum gauges continuously monitor
pressures across all chambers.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$18071e54-1aee-4bef-a5f5-d90198210139h
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhX␀␀ultra-high vacuum (~10II Torr). Gate valves isolate the subsystems, and vacuum gauges continuously monitor
pressures across all chambers.
2.7 High-Voltage System
The high-voltage system provides acceleration potentials up to 200 kV inside an insulated terminal. Terminal voltage,
extraction voltage, and suppression power supplies are managed by a dedicated HV controller. Hardwired interlocks
disable high-voltage generation if vacuum thresholds are violated or access panel switches are tripped.
2.8 Safety Systems and Interlockshh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$8e8334be-6a9e-4c4c-97fa-c0b64a36ef0dh
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXö␀␀IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual | Revision A | PrecisionBeam Technologies

Personnel and equipment safety are maintained through a distributed interlock system. The interlock loop monitors
toxic gas detectors (for Arsine and Phosphine leaks), radiation levels (X-ray monitoring near the high-voltage column),
vacuum pressures, cooling water flow, and the Emergency Master Off (EMO) buttons. If any safety threshold is
exceeded, the beam shutter is immediately closed, and high voltage is tripped.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$463f62bd-bc28-4f45-a9b1-3afb4b0289c8h

Chapter 3 â Communication Configuration
3.1 HSMS Communication Parameters
The HSMS interface on the IMP-HE2000 operates in Passive mode, meaning the tool listens for an incoming
connection from the factory host. The default TCP port is 5020. Standard timeout parameters (T3, T5, T6, T7, and T8)
are set to SEMI E37 defaults. These values can be modified locally on the tool's engineering panel or remotely via
SECS-II messages.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'HSMS Parameters', for the complete list of network
settings, IP addresses, port configuration, and timeout limits.
3.2 Device Configuration and VID Ranges
The IMP-HE2000 is represented as a single logical SECS-II device with DeviceID = 1. To organize the large number of
variables, events, and alarms, VIDs are partitioned into distinct ranges based on subsystem and variable type. Forhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$4aae686c-00f6-4a46-9c55-9c7f5c7d94eah
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXw␀␀variables, events, and alarms, VIDs are partitioned into distinct ranges based on subsystem and variable type. For
instance, Global System Variables occupy VIDs 1000â1049, Ion Source Variables occupy 1050â1099, and Data
Variables are assigned to the 2000+ range.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'VID Range Map', for the complete partitioning table and
subsystem allocations.
3.3 Tool Identity Block
The tool maintains static hardware and firmware configuration details in its non-volatile memory. This identity block
contains parameters such as the unique Tool ID, serial number, firmware revision, and physical limits (e.g., energy
and current range). These parameters can be queried by the host during initial online handshaking.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Tool Identity', for the detailed equipment metadata and
version strings.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$ba14c621-101e-47a5-bd9a-4304b81a68abh
)}(h

Chapter 4 â Status Variables (SV) â Description
Status Variables (SVs) represent continuously updated, real-time parameters monitored by the IMP-HE2000 control
computer. The host can poll these variables at any time using S1F3/F4 messages or include them in periodic trace
definitions (S2F23) or linked event reports (S2F35).
4.1 Global System Variables
Global variables track tool-wide states, GEM control states, and system-wide safety interlocks. These variables help
the host verify the current operating mode (e.g., IDLE, IMPLANTING) and ensure safety conditions are met before
starting a run.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Global System', for the complete list of global
variables, including SystemStatus, ControlState, and EMOStatus.
4.2 Ion Source Variables
Ion source variables monitor the health and discharge characteristics of the Freeman plasma source. Parametershh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$e4b28b5c-a33d-4b4c-9eb1-3de711fd1752h
)}(h
}(hh¢h}(hKhhhhhhhhhK	hKuhX␀␀variables, including SystemStatus, ControlState, and EMOStatus.
4.2 Ion Source Variables
Ion source variables monitor the health and discharge characteristics of the Freeman plasma source. Parameters
include arc current, filament current, filament voltage, extraction voltage, gas flow rate, and gas species. These values
are refreshed every 500 ms.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Ion Source', for all source-related SVs.
4.3 Beamline Variables
Beamline variables monitor ion beam transport and beam qualities, such as mass analyzer coil current, beam energy,
resolved Faraday cup current, electrostatic scan frequencies, spot sizes, and beam parallelism. These are critical to
verify that the ion beam is properly tuned and aligned before implanting the wafer.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Beamline', for the beamline variables list.
4.4 End Station Variableshh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$6be80c4b-5b01-4df3-9c65-917dd648a64eh
)}(h
}(hh©h}(hKhhhhhhhhhK	hKuhX½␀␀Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Beamline', for the beamline variables list.
4.4 End Station Variables
End station variables track process chamber parameters during implantation, including platen tilt/twist angles, wafer
clamp status, backside helium cooling flow, and real-time dose accumulation. Fast updates (200 ms) are provided for
critical dose and beam current parameters.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - End Station', for end station SV details.
4.5 Wafer Handler Variables
Wafer handler variables track the robot state, robot end-effector positions, load lock chamber pressure, load lock
pump/vent states, pre-aligner notch angle, and FOUP wafer mapping counts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Wafer Handler', for handling SVs.
4.6 Vacuum System Variables
Vacuum system variables monitor pressures in the beamline, process chamber, and source chamber, as well ashh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$82c8e64f-c931-4d6f-af5c-98426d81b339h
)}(h
}(hh°h}(hKhhhhhhhhhK	hKuhXL␀␀4.6 Vacuum System Variables
Vacuum system variables monitor pressures in the beamline, process chamber, and source chamber, as well as
turbomolecular pump speeds, cryopump cold-head temperature, and isolation gate valve positions.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Vacuum System', for vacuum SVs.
4.7 High-Voltage and Power Variables
High-voltage variables monitor terminal acceleration voltage, suppression voltage, extraction voltage, and power

Chapter 5 â Data Variables (DV) â Description
Data Variables (DVs) differ from Status Variables in that their values are event-dependent. They represent process
setup targets and post-process results (such as lot ID, recipe settings, measured dose, uniformity, and particle
counts). These values are updated at specific event triggers (like ImplantStart and ImplantEnd) and are typically read
by the host inside linked reports rather than polled during idle periods.
5.1 Recipe and Implant Target Variables
These variables capture the target process parameters defined in the active recipe, including the Target Species,
Target Energy, Target Dose, and Target Platen Tilt/Twist angles. They are updated when a recipe is loaded or an
implant run starts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Recipe and Implant Targets', for recipe DVs.
5.2 Process Result and Metrology Variableshh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$dbbef2e8-dfd5-4a94-9c67-1a998767288dh

}(hhÅh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhX␀␀implant run starts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Recipe and Implant Targets', for recipe DVs.
5.2 Process Result and Metrology Variables
Post-process variables contain metrology and quality assurance results for the most recently processed wafer, such
as actual dose delivered, measured dose uniformity, average beam current, implant duration, maximum wafer
temperature, ellipsometry results, and the process outcome (PASS/FAIL). These variables are updated when the
wafer processing ends or is aborted.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Process Results', for results and metrology DVs.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$ee67958c-7cda-4915-9fd0-a60d2b286287h

Chapter 6 â Collection Events (CEID) â Description
Collection Events (CEIDs) represent milestones in the equipment's physical and logical workflow. When an event
occurs, the equipment sends an S6F11 Event Report message containing linked reports to the host. The host can
dynamically enable or disable reporting for individual event IDs using the S2F37 message.
6.1 Implant Lifecycle Events
Implant lifecycle events track progress during wafer processing. The primary lifecycle events are ImplantStart,
ImplantEnd, and ImplantAbort. These events allow the host to track processing times and receive detailed
post-implant results immediately after a wafer is processed.
6.2 Beam Tuning Events
Beam tuning events notify the host of beam preparation progress. They include BeamTuneStart, BeamTuneComplete,
BeamLost, SourceIgnition, SourceExtinguish, and SourceFault. These events help the host monitor source stabilityhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$0f17ee3d-aead-4855-9b6b-5b27934c8a82h

and track beam setup durations.

Chapter 7 â Reports (RPTID) â Description
Reports (RPTIDs) are host-defined or factory-default structures that group multiple variables. By linking reports to
events, the host receives only the relevant parameters when an event occurs, minimising network traffic and
processing overhead. Report definition is managed via S2F33, and linking is performed via S2F35.
7.1 Standard Linked Reports
The IMP-HE2000 defines 14 standard reports, including RPT_ImplantStart, RPT_ImplantEnd, RPT_BeamStatus,
RPT_WaferLoad, RPT_AlarmEvent, RPT_SourceStatus, and RPT_VacuumStatus. These reports group relevant
status and data variables to provide a complete status update at the moment an event is triggered.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Reports', for details of all default reports and their
variables.

7.2 ReportâEvent Linking
The equipment controller maintains a default linking configuration to provide standard GEM reports out-of-the-box. For
example, the ImplantStart event is linked to RPT_ImplantStart and RPT_BeamStatus, ensuring the host receives both
process targets and beam parameters at start.

Chapter 8 â Alarm Management â Description
Alarms are generated when an operational parameter exceeds safe limits or a hardware failure is detected. Alarms are
reported to the host immediately via S5F1 messages. In addition, an AlarmSet event is triggered, allowing the host to
receive a linked report with system status details. Host control systems should monitor alarms to interlock factory
automation tasks.
8.1 Critical Alarms
Critical Alarms represent severe faults that cause an immediate process abort, close the beam shutter, and trip high
voltage. Examples include Source_ArcFault, Source_GasLeak, Beam_EnergyContamination, EndStn_DoseOverrun,
HV_ArcOver, Vacuum leaks, and EMO activation.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Critical', for the complete list of critical alarms,
codes, and linked SVIDs.
8.2 Warning Alarmshh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$e97fd6d3-be37-4023-8cb2-2008029d0a5ah
)}(h
}(hhïh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXÊ␀␀Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Critical', for the complete list of critical alarms,
codes, and linked SVIDs.
8.2 Warning Alarms
Warning Alarms notify the operator of degraded performance or upcoming maintenance needs without aborting the
active process. Examples include Source_FilamentDegraded, Beam_CurrentInstability, EndStn_CoolantFlowLow,
cryopump temperature drift, and pending PM counters.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Warning', for all warning alarms.
8.3 Alarm Response Procedures (Detailed)
When an alarm is received by the host, the factory control system should log the Alarm ID and text, check linked
variables (e.g., pressure or temperature SVIDs) to assess severity, and notify the operator. Critical alarms require
manual operator investigation, hardware repair (if needed), and a RESET_FAULT command to clear the error state.
Step-by-step recovery details are provided in Appendix C.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$9ef75231-852b-46eb-9c9a-4ddf23bfaf5dh

Chapter 9 â Remote Commands (RCMD) â Description
Remote Commands allow the host to control equipment operations using S2F41 messages. Commands can include
parameters (e.g., recipe name, wafer ID) passed as CPNAME/CPVAL pairs. The equipment replies with S2F42
containing the HCACK code indicating acceptance or rejection.
9.1 Process Control Commands
Process control commands manage the implant run. They include START_IMPLANT (starts the run with specified
RECIPE_ID and WAFER_ID parameters), ABORT_IMPLANT (aborts the run immediately), PAUSE_IMPLANT, and
RESUME_IMPLANT. These commands allow full automated operation of wafer lots.
9.2 Beam and Source Commands
These commands manage beam preparation, including TUNE_BEAM (initiates tuning for species and energy
setpoints), SOURCE_ON (ignites source plasma with specified gas), SOURCE_OFF, HV_ON, and HV_OFF. Thesehh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$2ce76560-85f6-417a-afb4-e52ffabed1d2h
)}(h
}(hhýh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhK uhXb␀␀setpoints), SOURCE_ON (ignites source plasma with specified gas), SOURCE_OFF, HV_ON, and HV_OFF. These
allow the host to prepare the tool prior to starting a process lot.
9.3 Maintenance and Configuration Commands
Maintenance commands assist with calibration and troubleshooting. They include LOAD_RECIPE, DELETE_RECIPE,
ENTER_MAINTENANCE, EXIT_MAINTENANCE, RESET_FAULT (clears fault state to IDLE), SET_CLOCK,
RESET_PM_COUNTER, PUMP_DOWN_LOADLOCK, and VENT_LOADLOCK.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Remote Commands', for all command names, parameter
requirements, and resulting events.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$8262741b-aa9b-48b0-ae13-4fcb4363f2cdh

Chapter 10 â Equipment State Machine
10.1 State Definitions
The IMP-HE2000 process state machine represents the physical status of the implanter. The primary states are: IDLE
(ready to accept commands), SETTING_UP (recipe loaded, source warming, beam tuning active), BEAM_READY
(beam stable, waiting for wafer), LOADING (transferring wafer to platen), ALIGNING (moving platen to tilt/twist
angles), IMPLANTING (beam on, scanning, dose accumulating), UNLOADING (wafer returning to load lock),
COMPLETED (run finished), FAULT (stopped due to alarm), and MAINTENANCE (servicing active).
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'State Definitions', for definitions of all process states.
10.2 Transition Logic
Transitions occur in response to host commands (manual) or equipment events (automatic). For example, receiving ahh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$edaa7101-0512-4c3d-991f-93ebeb36da13h

Transitions occur in response to host commands (manual) or equipment events (automatic). For example, receiving a
START_IMPLANT command triggers a transition from IDLE to SETTING_UP. Once beam tuning completes, the tool
automatically transitions to BEAM_READY. Critical alarms trigger an automatic transition from any active state to
FAULT.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'State Transitions', for the complete transition table,
including source states, destination states, triggers, and manual/auto classifications.

Appendix B â Operational Scenarios (Prose)
B.1 Communication and Configuration Setup
1. Host connection: Host initiates a TCP connection to the tool IP and port 5020. Once established, host sends
S1F13 (Establish Communications).
2. Tool acknowledge: The tool verifies network parameters and replies with S1F14 (COMMACK=0x00). The GEM
Control State transitions to ON-LINE.
3. Report definitions: Host sends S2F33 to define standard reports (e.g., linking report 3101 to variables for beam
and dose). The tool replies with S2F34 (DRACK=0x00).
4. Link reports to events: Host sends S2F35 to link reports to events (e.g., linking event 3001 to report 3101). Tool
replies with S2F36 (LRACK=0x00).
5. Enable event notifications: Host sends S2F37 to enable event notifications for lot tracking. Tool replies with
S2F38 (ERACK=0x00).
B.2 Successful Implant Process Runhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$ee965c94-f5b2-45a0-a437-4b3f6038f039h
)}(h
}(hjX␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhK-uhXã␀␀5. Enable event notifications: Host sends S2F37 to enable event notifications for lot tracking. Tool replies with
S2F38 (ERACK=0x00).
B.2 Successful Implant Process Run
1. Recipe upload: Host uploads process recipe 'B_120K_1E15' using S7F3. Tool replies with S7F4 (ACKC7=0x00).

Appendix C â Alarm Recovery Procedures (Detailed Step-by-Step)
ALID 4001 â Source_ArcFault
1. Tool automatically shuts off plasma and closes the beam shutter. High voltage remains disabled.
2. Host receives S5F1 for ALID 4001. Operator should verify SVID 1051 (arc current) and SVID 1052 (arc voltage).
3. Inspect tungsten filament and arc chamber for degradation. Filament operational hours are checked via SVID 1061.
4. If filament is thin or broken, perform source maintenance and reset source lifetime hours counter.
5. After hardware check, send RESET_FAULT RCMD to return to IDLE state.
ALID 4002 â Source_GasLeak
1. Hardwired interlocks close toxic gas cabinet pneumatic valves immediately and trigger facility exhaust alarms.
2. Host receives S5F1 for ALID 4002. Evacuate all personnel from the gas box and tool bay immediately.
3. Notify facility safety officer. Do not attempt local tool reset.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$cb88e6ab-c198-482b-a5f4-b091bc0ec40dh

3. Notify facility safety officer. Do not attempt local tool reset.
4. Verify leak condition using facility ambient gas monitors.
5. Once cleared, reset facility safety loops, then send RESET_FAULT RCMD from host.
ALID 4005 â EndStn_DoseOverrun
1. Tool closes the electrostatic beam shutter, terminates wafer scanning, and transitions to FAULT.
2. Host receives S5F1 for ALID 4005 and ImplantAbort event report.
3. Check actual dose delivered (DVID 2051) against recipe target (DVID 2008). Check beam stability (DVID 2062).
4. Calibrate dose Faraday cups. Check dose integrator electronics.
5. Send RESET_FAULT RCMD, unload the damaged wafer, and restart process with a test wafer.

1. Beam shutter is closed, platen mechanical scanning is stopped, and tool transitions to FAULT.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$27657973-a8e7-4f78-a7dd-6aec87fe89d0h

1. Beam shutter is closed, platen mechanical scanning is stopped, and tool transitions to FAULT.
2. Check measured wafer temperature (SVID 1159). Monitor until wafer cools down below 50Â°C.
3. Check backside Helium coolant pressure (SVID 1163) and coolant flow rate (SVID 1162).

Chapter 1 â Introduction
1.1 Purpose and Scope
This manual describes the operation, architecture, and SECS/GEM host interface of the IMP-HE2000 High-Energy
Medium-Current Ion Implanter manufactured by PrecisionBeam Technologies. It covers equipment subsystems,
process workflows, state machine behaviour, alarm handling, and remote command capabilities. For all tabular data â
including variable IDs, event codes, alarm definitions, report structures, and state transitions â refer to the companion
workbook: IMP_HE2000_Variable_Tables.xlsx.
1.2 How to Use This Manual
This manual is the prose companion to the Variable Tables workbook. The manual explains HOW the equipment
works and WHY variables/events/alarms exist. The workbook provides the WHAT â exact IDs, types, ranges, and
linkages. Together they form the complete SECS/GEM Interface Control Document (ICD).

Chapter 2 â Equipment Overview
2.1 System Architecture
The PrecisionBeam IMP-HE2000 is a high-energy, medium-current ion implanter designed specifically for 300 mm
silicon wafer processing in modern semiconductor fabs. The system consists of seven primary hardware subsystems:
the Ion Source, the Beamline, the End Station, the Wafer Handler, the Vacuum System, the High-Voltage System, and
the central Control System. All subsystems interface directly with the equipment controller, which hosts the
SECS/GEM software stack and manages the factory automation link over HSMS-SS.
2.2 Ion Source Subsystem
The ion source is a Freeman-type hot cathode source designed for high plasma stability. Precursor gases (BFâ , PHâ ,
AsHâ , or Ar for setup) are introduced into the arc chamber via mass flow controllers. A tungsten filament is heated tohh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$fbc438fb-ddef-46f2-afbc-4a1e51f2f706h
)}(h
}(hhgh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhX␀␀AsHâ , or Ar for setup) are introduced into the arc chamber via mass flow controllers. A tungsten filament is heated to
thermionic emission temperatures, and an electrical discharge (arc voltage) ignites a dense plasma inside the
chamber. An extraction electrode assembly pulls positive ions from the plasma aperture, forming a preliminary ion
beam. Real-time parameters include arc current, filament current, extraction voltage, and source gas pressure. The
filament and arc chamber have finite lifetimes and require periodic maintenance, tracked by local timers.
2.3 Beamline Subsystem
The beamline collimates, refines, and accelerates the extracted ion beam. An analyzer magnet acts as a mass
spectrometer, bending the ion path through a 90-degree arc. Since mass deflection is proportional to charge, only the
desired dopant species (e.g., Boron-11) passes through the resolving aperture, filtering out contaminants andhh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$85498de3-8a6f-4df9-9448-7adff245f61dh
)}(h
}(hhnh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhXå␀␀desired dopant species (e.g., Boron-11) passes through the resolving aperture, filtering out contaminants and
unwanted carrier species. The filtered beam is then accelerated or decelerated in the high-voltage column to match
recipe requirements. Electrostatic scan plates deflect the beam at high frequencies to create a uniform scanning
ribbon beam. Multi-point Faraday cups measure the beam current to ensure stability and parallelism.
2.4 End Station Subsystem
The end station houses the process chamber where wafers undergo ion implantation under high vacuum. A wafer is
held on an electrostatic chuck (platen) that provides Helium backside cooling to maintain wafer temperature below
critical photoresist degradation levels (typically < 120Â°C). The platen tilt and twist mechanisms position the wafer
relative to the incoming beam, avoiding crystal channeling. A Faraday cup array behind the platen measures the
actual dose in real-time, halting the implant when the target dose is achieved.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$68943ba4-575d-400b-984f-1f62f4472c46h
)}(h
}(hhuh}(hKhhhhhhhK
uhXæ␀␀relative to the incoming beam, avoiding crystal channeling. A Faraday cup array behind the platen measures the
actual dose in real-time, halting the implant when the target dose is achieved.
2.5 Wafer Handling Subsystem
The wafer handler manages wafer transfer between atmospheric and vacuum environments. It features two FOUP
load ports, an atmospheric transfer robot with a slot-mapping sensor, an optical notch pre-aligner, a vacuum load lock
chamber, and a vacuum transfer arm. Wafers are transferred individually to the process platen, maintaining high
vacuum in the process chamber during lot processing.
2.6 Vacuum System
High-vacuum integrity is vital to prevent ion beam scattering and wafer contamination. The beamline is evacuated by
dual turbomolecular pumps backed by dry scroll pumps. The end station process chamber uses a cryogenic pump for
ultra-high vacuum (~10â â  Torr). Gate valves isolate the subsystems, and vacuum gauges continuously monitor
pressures across all chambers.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$6ef192c7-bff9-448d-9570-abb16dac338ah
)}(h
}(hh|h}(hKhhhhhhhKuhX␀␀ultra-high vacuum (~10â â  Torr). Gate valves isolate the subsystems, and vacuum gauges continuously monitor
pressures across all chambers.
2.7 High-Voltage System
The high-voltage system provides acceleration potentials up to 200 kV inside an insulated terminal. Terminal voltage,
extraction voltage, and suppression power supplies are managed by a dedicated HV controller. Hardwired interlocks
disable high-voltage generation if vacuum thresholds are violated or access panel switches are tripped.

Chapter 3 â Communication Configuration
3.1 HSMS Communication Parameters
The HSMS interface on the IMP-HE2000 operates in Passive mode, meaning the tool listens for an incoming
connection from the factory host. The default TCP port is 5020. Standard timeout parameters (T3, T5, T6, T7, and T8)
are set to SEMI E37 defaults. These values can be modified locally on the tool's engineering panel or remotely via
SECS-II messages.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'HSMS Parameters', for the complete list of network
settings, IP addresses, port configuration, and timeout limits.
3.2 Device Configuration and VID Ranges
The IMP-HE2000 is represented as a single logical SECS-II device with DeviceID = 1. To organize the large number of
variables, events, and alarms, VIDs are partitioned into distinct ranges based on subsystem and variable type. Forhh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$803c36e5-0f83-49ca-85d2-311ea6cc93c9h
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhXw␀␀variables, events, and alarms, VIDs are partitioned into distinct ranges based on subsystem and variable type. For
instance, Global System Variables occupy VIDs 1000â1049, Ion Source Variables occupy 1050â1099, and Data
Variables are assigned to the 2000+ range.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'VID Range Map', for the complete partitioning table and
subsystem allocations.
3.3 Tool Identity Block
The tool maintains static hardware and firmware configuration details in its non-volatile memory. This identity block
contains parameters such as the unique Tool ID, serial number, firmware revision, and physical limits (e.g., energy
and current range). These parameters can be queried by the host during initial online handshaking.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Tool Identity', for the detailed equipment metadata and
version strings.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$aa934987-291e-4d46-86b7-b5a7994f4e14h

Chapter 4 â Status Variables (SV) â Description
Status Variables (SVs) represent continuously updated, real-time parameters monitored by the IMP-HE2000 control
computer. The host can poll these variables at any time using S1F3/F4 messages or include them in periodic trace
definitions (S2F23) or linked event reports (S2F35).
4.1 Global System Variables
Global variables track tool-wide states, GEM control states, and system-wide safety interlocks. These variables help
the host verify the current operating mode (e.g., IDLE, IMPLANTING) and ensure safety conditions are met before
starting a run.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Global System', for the complete list of global
variables, including SystemStatus, ControlState, and EMOStatus.
4.2 Ion Source Variables
Ion source variables monitor the health and discharge characteristics of the Freeman plasma source. Parametershh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$c0d387a7-a561-4162-96ee-88a1ac88d063h
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhX␀␀variables, including SystemStatus, ControlState, and EMOStatus.
4.2 Ion Source Variables
Ion source variables monitor the health and discharge characteristics of the Freeman plasma source. Parameters
include arc current, filament current, filament voltage, extraction voltage, gas flow rate, and gas species. These values
are refreshed every 500 ms.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Ion Source', for all source-related SVs.
4.3 Beamline Variables
Beamline variables monitor ion beam transport and beam qualities, such as mass analyzer coil current, beam energy,
resolved Faraday cup current, electrostatic scan frequencies, spot sizes, and beam parallelism. These are critical to
verify that the ion beam is properly tuned and aligned before implanting the wafer.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Beamline', for the beamline variables list.
4.4 End Station Variableshh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$4205dffa-977b-4590-bb62-d2d025395b9ch

4.4 End Station Variables
End station variables track process chamber parameters during implantation, including platen tilt/twist angles, wafer
clamp status, backside helium cooling flow, and real-time dose accumulation. Fast updates (200 ms) are provided for
critical dose and beam current parameters.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - End Station', for end station SV details.
4.5 Wafer Handler Variables
Wafer handler variables track the robot state, robot end-effector positions, load lock chamber pressure, load lock
pump/vent states, pre-aligner notch angle, and FOUP wafer mapping counts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Wafer Handler', for handling SVs.

turbomolecular pump speeds, cryopump cold-head temperature, and isolation gate valve positions.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Vacuum System', for vacuum SVs.

Chapter 5 â Data Variables (DV) â Description
Data Variables (DVs) differ from Status Variables in that their values are event-dependent. They represent process
setup targets and post-process results (such as lot ID, recipe settings, measured dose, uniformity, and particle
counts). These values are updated at specific event triggers (like ImplantStart and ImplantEnd) and are typically read
by the host inside linked reports rather than polled during idle periods.
5.1 Recipe and Implant Target Variables
These variables capture the target process parameters defined in the active recipe, including the Target Species,
Target Energy, Target Dose, and Target Platen Tilt/Twist angles. They are updated when a recipe is loaded or an
implant run starts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Recipe and Implant Targets', for recipe DVs.
5.2 Process Result and Metrology Variableshh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$41b2d64c-3f19-4af7-8368-25938e19fb55h
)}(h
}(hhÂh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhX␀␀implant run starts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Recipe and Implant Targets', for recipe DVs.
5.2 Process Result and Metrology Variables
Post-process variables contain metrology and quality assurance results for the most recently processed wafer, such
as actual dose delivered, measured dose uniformity, average beam current, implant duration, maximum wafer
temperature, ellipsometry results, and the process outcome (PASS/FAIL). These variables are updated when the
wafer processing ends or is aborted.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Process Results', for results and metrology DVs.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$e1e8e4b9-613f-4b2c-a054-ca3d73b8b964h
)}(h
}(hhÉh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhXé␀␀IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual | Revision A | PrecisionBeam Technologies

Chapter 6 â Collection Events (CEID) â Description
Collection Events (CEIDs) represent milestones in the equipment's physical and logical workflow. When an event
occurs, the equipment sends an S6F11 Event Report message containing linked reports to the host. The host can
dynamically enable or disable reporting for individual event IDs using the S2F37 message.
6.1 Implant Lifecycle Events
Implant lifecycle events track progress during wafer processing. The primary lifecycle events are ImplantStart,
ImplantEnd, and ImplantAbort. These events allow the host to track processing times and receive detailed
post-implant results immediately after a wafer is processed.
6.2 Beam Tuning Events

Chapter 7 â Reports (RPTID) â Description
Reports (RPTIDs) are host-defined or factory-default structures that group multiple variables. By linking reports to
events, the host receives only the relevant parameters when an event occurs, minimising network traffic and
processing overhead. Report definition is managed via S2F33, and linking is performed via S2F35.
7.1 Standard Linked Reports
The IMP-HE2000 defines 14 standard reports, including RPT_ImplantStart, RPT_ImplantEnd, RPT_BeamStatus,
RPT_WaferLoad, RPT_AlarmEvent, RPT_SourceStatus, and RPT_VacuumStatus. These reports group relevant
status and data variables to provide a complete status update at the moment an event is triggered.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Reports', for details of all default reports and their
variables.

7.2 ReportâEvent Linking

Chapter 8 â Alarm Management â Description
Alarms are generated when an operational parameter exceeds safe limits or a hardware failure is detected. Alarms are
reported to the host immediately via S5F1 messages. In addition, an AlarmSet event is triggered, allowing the host to
receive a linked report with system status details. Host control systems should monitor alarms to interlock factory
automation tasks.
8.1 Critical Alarms
Critical Alarms represent severe faults that cause an immediate process abort, close the beam shutter, and trip high
voltage. Examples include Source_ArcFault, Source_GasLeak, Beam_EnergyContamination, EndStn_DoseOverrun,
HV_ArcOver, Vacuum leaks, and EMO activation.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Critical', for the complete list of critical alarms,
codes, and linked SVIDs.
8.2 Warning Alarmshh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$680969e8-08e0-4ab0-affb-9b1c9cec5632h
)}(h
}(hhìh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhXÊ␀␀Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Critical', for the complete list of critical alarms,
codes, and linked SVIDs.
8.2 Warning Alarms
Warning Alarms notify the operator of degraded performance or upcoming maintenance needs without aborting the
active process. Examples include Source_FilamentDegraded, Beam_CurrentInstability, EndStn_CoolantFlowLow,
cryopump temperature drift, and pending PM counters.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Alarms - Warning', for all warning alarms.
8.3 Alarm Response Procedures (Detailed)
When an alarm is received by the host, the factory control system should log the Alarm ID and text, check linked
variables (e.g., pressure or temperature SVIDs) to assess severity, and notify the operator. Critical alarms require
manual operator investigation, hardware repair (if needed), and a RESET_FAULT command to clear the error state.
Step-by-step recovery details are provided in Appendix C.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$ea0d429f-1bbc-47b0-a9e4-200f465264e6h

Chapter 9 â Remote Commands (RCMD) â Description
Remote Commands allow the host to control equipment operations using S2F41 messages. Commands can include
parameters (e.g., recipe name, wafer ID) passed as CPNAME/CPVAL pairs. The equipment replies with S2F42
containing the HCACK code indicating acceptance or rejection.
9.1 Process Control Commands
Process control commands manage the implant run. They include START_IMPLANT (starts the run with specified
RECIPE_ID and WAFER_ID parameters), ABORT_IMPLANT (aborts the run immediately), PAUSE_IMPLANT, and
RESUME_IMPLANT. These commands allow full automated operation of wafer lots.
9.2 Beam and Source Commands
These commands manage beam preparation, including TUNE_BEAM (initiates tuning for species and energy
setpoints), SOURCE_ON (ignites source plasma with specified gas), SOURCE_OFF, HV_ON, and HV_OFF. Thesehh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$371a29e6-b61e-424c-a063-88b3836cd15bh
)}(h

allow the host to prepare the tool prior to starting a process lot.
9.3 Maintenance and Configuration Commands
Maintenance commands assist with calibration and troubleshooting. They include LOAD_RECIPE, DELETE_RECIPE,
ENTER_MAINTENANCE, EXIT_MAINTENANCE, RESET_FAULT (clears fault state to IDLE), SET_CLOCK,
RESET_PM_COUNTER, PUMP_DOWN_LOADLOCK, and VENT_LOADLOCK.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Remote Commands', for all command names, parameter
requirements, and resulting events.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$bf23931c-0bed-42f7-8061-4ed9e0db7d54h

Chapter 10 â Equipment State Machine
10.1 State Definitions
The IMP-HE2000 process state machine represents the physical status of the implanter. The primary states are: IDLE
(ready to accept commands), SETTING_UP (recipe loaded, source warming, beam tuning active), BEAM_READY
(beam stable, waiting for wafer), LOADING (transferring wafer to platen), ALIGNING (moving platen to tilt/twist
angles), IMPLANTING (beam on, scanning, dose accumulating), UNLOADING (wafer returning to load lock),
COMPLETED (run finished), FAULT (stopped due to alarm), and MAINTENANCE (servicing active).
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'State Definitions', for definitions of all process states.
10.2 Transition Logic
Transitions occur in response to host commands (manual) or equipment events (automatic). For example, receiving ahh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$fbd5796e-c25d-4417-89a4-163b4205e253h

Transitions occur in response to host commands (manual) or equipment events (automatic). For example, receiving a
START_IMPLANT command triggers a transition from IDLE to SETTING_UP. Once beam tuning completes, the tool
automatically transitions to BEAM_READY. Critical alarms trigger an automatic transition from any active state to
FAULT.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'State Transitions', for the complete transition table,
including source states, destination states, triggers, and manual/auto classifications.

Appendix B â Operational Scenarios (Prose)
B.1 Communication and Configuration Setup
1. Host connection: Host initiates a TCP connection to the tool IP and port 5020. Once established, host sends
S1F13 (Establish Communications).
2. Tool acknowledge: The tool verifies network parameters and replies with S1F14 (COMMACK=0x00). The GEM
Control State transitions to ON-LINE.
3. Report definitions: Host sends S2F33 to define standard reports (e.g., linking report 3101 to variables for beam
and dose). The tool replies with S2F34 (DRACK=0x00).
4. Link reports to events: Host sends S2F35 to link reports to events (e.g., linking event 3001 to report 3101). Tool
replies with S2F36 (LRACK=0x00).
5. Enable event notifications: Host sends S2F37 to enable event notifications for lot tracking. Tool replies with
S2F38 (ERACK=0x00).
B.2 Successful Implant Process Runhh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$c71eff0f-9201-47f2-9d31-256a476ce02eh

S2F38 (ERACK=0x00).
B.2 Successful Implant Process Run
1. Recipe upload: Host uploads process recipe 'B_120K_1E15' using S7F3. Tool replies with S7F4 (ACKC7=0x00).
2. Implant start command: Host sends S2F41 with command START_IMPLANT and parameters
RECIPE_ID='B_120K_1E15', WAFER_ID='WFR-B24', SLOT_NUMBER=5. Tool checks safety interlocks and replies
with S2F42 (HCACK=0x00).
3. Tuning and load lock pump: Tool transitions to SETTING_UP state. The source plasma is ignited, and the load
lock pumps down. Once vacuum and beam parameters are ready, tool transitions to BEAM_READY.
4. Wafer loading and alignment: The wafer is loaded onto the platen, and the platen moves to the tilt/twist angles.
The tool sends S6F11 for WaferLoaded_EndStation (CEID 3010).
5. Implant active: The beam shutter opens, and implantation begins. Tool sends S6F11 for ImplantStart (CEID 3001).hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$071caff1-6542-47da-93ba-a8f424e820adh
)}(h
}(hj\␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhK.uhX«␀␀The tool sends S6F11 for WaferLoaded_EndStation (CEID 3010).
5. Implant active: The beam shutter opens, and implantation begins. Tool sends S6F11 for ImplantStart (CEID 3001).
6. Dose achieved: When target dose is achieved (1e15 ions/cmÂ²), the beam shutter closes. Tool sends S6F11 for
ImplantEnd (CEID 3002) containing report 3102 with delivered dose, uniformity, and PASS result.
7. Wafer unload: The platen returns to home position, and the robot transfers the wafer back to the FOUP. Tool sends
S6F11 for WaferUnloaded_EndStation (CEID 3011).

Appendix C â Alarm Recovery Procedures (Detailed Step-by-Step)
ALID 4001 â Source_ArcFault
1. Tool automatically shuts off plasma and closes the beam shutter. High voltage remains disabled.
2. Host receives S5F1 for ALID 4001. Operator should verify SVID 1051 (arc current) and SVID 1052 (arc voltage).
3. Inspect tungsten filament and arc chamber for degradation. Filament operational hours are checked via SVID 1061.
4. If filament is thin or broken, perform source maintenance and reset source lifetime hours counter.
5. After hardware check, send RESET_FAULT RCMD to return to IDLE state.
ALID 4002 â Source_GasLeak
1. Hardwired interlocks close toxic gas cabinet pneumatic valves immediately and trigger facility exhaust alarms.

Chapter 1 — Introduction
This document is the authoritative SECS/GEM Interface Control Document (ICD) for the NanoDyne
ETCH-Z500 Reactive Ion Etch System. It defines every aspect of the host-to-equipment communication
interface required to integrate this tool into a factory automation environment under the SEMI E30 Generic
Equipment Model standard. Host software engineers, MES integration teams, and equipment qualification
engineers should use this document as the primary reference for all variable polling, event subscriptions, alarm
handling, remote command sequences, and state machine behaviour.
The ETCH-Z500 is a single-chamber capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) etch system designed for 300 mm
silicon wafer processing. The tool is capable of oxide, nitride, and polysilicon etch processes using CF4/O2/Ar
chemistry. A 13.56 MHz RF generator drives the upper electrode, and a separate bias supply controls the
wafer chuck potential independently. This dual-frequency architecture allows independent control of ion energy
and plasma density, which is critical for achieving the etch selectivity and profile control required at advanced
process nodes.
1.1 Purpose and Scope
This ICD covers the complete set of SECS/GEM objects exposed by the ETCH-Z500 controller: Status
Variables (SVs), Data Variables (DVs), Collection Events (CEIDs), Reports (RPTIDs), Alarms, Remote
Commands (RCMDs), and the equipment state machine. It also documents the HSMS communication
parameters, the VID address space layout, and the GEM compliance posture of the equipment. Process recipe
content, calibration procedures, and hardware maintenance are outside the scope of this document and are
covered in the ETCH-Z500 Process Manual (ND-ETCH-Z500-PM-001).
1.2 Communication Architecture
The ETCH-Z500 uses HSMS-SS (High-Speed Message Services, Single Session) as its transport layer,
operating in Passive mode on TCP port 5011. The equipment listens for an incoming connection from the
factory host; the host is always the TCP client. Once the TCP session is established, the host must initiate the
SECS/GEM session by sending S1F13 (Establish Communications Request). The equipment replies with
S1F14 containing COMMACK=0x00 on success. The host should subscribe to collection events and define its
report structures immediately after a successful S1F14.

Chapter 2 — Status Variables (SV)
Status Variables represent the real-time operating state of the ETCH-Z500 and its subsystems. The host may
read any SV at any time by sending S1F3 (Selected Equipment Status Request) with the desired list of SVIDs;
the equipment replies with S1F4 containing the current values. SVs may also be included in periodic trace
collections configured via S2F23, or delivered automatically inside linked reports when a Collection Event fires
via S6F11.
All SVIDs are read-only unless explicitly marked (R/W) in the table below. Update rates indicate how frequently
the equipment controller refreshes the internal value; the host should not poll faster than the stated rate for
time-sensitive variables such as chamber pressure or RF power. For real-time monitoring of process variables,
the recommended approach is to configure S2F23 trace collection at an appropriate sample interval rather than
issuing repeated S1F3 polls.
