Chapter 3 — Data Variables (DV)
Data Variables differ from Status Variables in that their values are event-dependent rather than continuously
updated. A DV holds the value captured at the most recently completed event context — for example,
EtchDepth (DVID 2004) contains the measured etch depth of the last processed wafer and retains that value
until the next wafer completes processing. DVs should not be polled during idle periods; their values are only
meaningful after a relevant event has fired.
The recommended host practice is to receive DVs through linked reports: configure the desired DVIDs into a
report using S2F33, link that report to the relevant Collection Event using S2F35, and enable event reporting
using S2F37. The equipment will then automatically push the correct post-process values in the S6F11 Event
Report Send at exactly the moment they become valid.
DVs 2001–2009 represent process identity and outcome variables. DVs 2010–2012 capture the recipe target
setpoints that were active at process start, providing full traceability of what was commanded versus what was
measured.

Chapter 4 — Collection Events (CEID)
Collection Events are named milestones in the equipment's process and control lifecycle. When an event
occurs, the equipment sends an S6F11 (Event Report Send) message to the host containing the values of all
variables linked to that event through the active report configuration. The host acknowledges with S6F12.
Event reporting is enabled or disabled per-CEID using S2F37 (Enable/Disable Event Report). All events are
disabled at power-on and must be explicitly enabled by the host after establishing communications. At
minimum, the host should enable ProcessStart (3001), ProcessEnd (3002), WaferLoaded (3006),
WaferUnloaded (3007), and AlarmSet (3008) to support standard lot tracking and alarm management
workflows.

Chapter 5 — Alarm Definitions
The ETCH-Z500 alarm system continuously monitors critical process and safety parameters. When an alarm
condition is detected, the equipment immediately sends an S5F1 (Alarm Report Send) message containing the
Alarm ID, alarm text, and a set/clear flag. Simultaneously, an AlarmSet Collection Event (CEID 3008) fires,
delivering the linked system status report to the host.
Alarms are classified into two severity levels. Critical alarms represent conditions that pose a risk to personnel
safety, equipment integrity, or wafer integrity. On a critical alarm the equipment immediately aborts any active
process, cuts RF power, and transitions to the FAULT state. The tool cannot resume operation until the alarm is
acknowledged, the root cause resolved, and a RESET_FAULT RCMD is issued by the host. Warning alarms
indicate degraded conditions that do not immediately threaten safety but may affect process quality if
unaddressed. They are logged and reported without aborting the process, unless they persist beyond a defined
tolerance window.
5.1 Critical Alarms

5.3 Alarm Response Procedures
The table below summarises recommended host-side and operator responses. Detailed step-by-step recovery
procedures are in the ETCH-Z500 Process Manual (ND-ETCH-Z500-PM-001).
Alarm
Immediate Host Action
Recovery Steps
OverPressure
Send ABORT_PROCESS RCMD. Do not
vent the chamber.
Check throttle valve position and MFC calibration.
Verify recipe pressure setpoint is within the tool's
operating range. Issue RESET_FAULT once pressure
stabilises below limit.
PlasmaFailure
Log alarm. Poll SVIDs 1005, 1006, 1015 for
diagnostics.
Verify process pressure is within ignition range
(20–200 mTorr). Allow up to 2 automatic ignition
retries. If fault persists after 3 attempts, schedule RF
generator and match network PM.
EMO_Activated
Alert safety officer. Do not attempt remote
reset.
Identify and clear the EMO trigger condition. Perform
full safety walkdown and lockout/tagout clearance.
Physical EMO reset at the tool is required before
issuing RESET_FAULT.
PumpFault
Send ABORT_PROCESS RCMD. Monitor
pump temperature via SVID 1014.
Check pump cooling water supply flow. If bearing or
over-temperature fault, schedule pump replacement.
Do not restart until root cause is confirmed cleared.
RF_MatchFault
Log reflected power trend from SVID 1006.
Inspect match network capacitors and tuning range.
Run the match network self-calibration routine from the
equipment engineering panel. Replace match board
PCB if fault recurs.

Chapter 6 — Remote Commands (RCMD)
Remote Commands allow the factory host to initiate equipment actions using the S2F41 (Host Command
Send) message. The equipment validates each command and replies with S2F42 (Host Command
Acknowledge) containing an HCACK code. HCACK = 0x00 indicates the command was accepted; any
non-zero value indicates rejection, with the reason encoded in the CPACK field of the parameter acknowledge
list.
Commands that affect process state — such as START_PROCESS or ABORT_PROCESS — are only
accepted when the equipment is in ON-LINE REMOTE control state (ControlState SVID 1002 = 5). Commands
sent while the tool is in LOCAL mode will be rejected with HCACK = 0x02 (Cannot perform now). The host
should verify ControlState before issuing process control commands. All command parameters are passed as
CPNAME/CPVAL pairs in the S2F41 body.

Chapter 7 — Equipment State Machine
The ETCH-Z500 process controller implements a deterministic state machine that governs all transitions
between operating modes. Understanding the state machine is essential for writing correct host automation
sequences, because many remote commands are only accepted in specific states. The GEM Control State
(SVID 1002), defined by SEMI E30, is a separate orthogonal state machine that governs the host-equipment
relationship and operates independently of the process state.
The equipment reports its current process state through SystemStatus (SVID 1001). The host can also track
state transitions event-by-event through the Collection Events defined in Chapter 4, which fire automatically as
the tool moves through its process sequence — eliminating the need for the host to poll SystemStatus during a
run.
7.1 State Definitions
State
Description
IDLE
Chamber is at or near atmospheric pressure, at ambient temperature, and fully ready to accept a new
process request. This is the normal resting state between wafer runs.
PUMPING
Vacuum pump-down sequence is in progress. The turbomolecular pump is running and chamber
pressure is decreasing toward the process base pressure target (<5 mTorr). No gas flow or RF
activity.
PURGE
Argon purge gas is flowing through the chamber to displace residual atmospheric contamination
before process gases are introduced. Pressure is controlled at the recipe purge setpoint.
PROCESSING
Active etch step is in progress. Process gases (CF4, O2, Ar) are flowing at recipe setpoints, RF
power is on, plasma is ignited and MATCHED, and the etch timer or endpoint algorithm is running.
COMPLETED
Etch run has finished successfully. The wafer remains on the chuck. The equipment waits for the host
command or robot action to initiate wafer unload.
VENT
Chamber is being vented to atmospheric pressure using a controlled N2 backfill. Entered
automatically after wafer unload to prepare the chamber for the next load cycle.
FAULT
A critical alarm has occurred and the process has been aborted. The chamber is in a safe but
non-operational state. A RESET_FAULT command is required after root cause resolution to return to
IDLE.
MAINTENANCE
Equipment is in maintenance mode following an ENTER_MAINTENANCE command. Process starts
are fully inhibited. Operator has safe access to chamber and gas system.

Chapter 8 — Reports (RPTID)
Reports define named collections of variables that are delivered to the host whenever a linked Collection Event
fires. The host configures reports using S2F33 (Define Report) to specify which variable IDs are grouped under
each RPTID, and uses S2F35 (Link Event Report) to associate each report with one or more CEIDs. This
mechanism ensures the MES receives exactly the data it needs at exactly the right moment — without
continuous polling.
The default report configuration described below is established by the equipment at power-on. The host may
redefine reports at any time using S2F33. Sending S2F33 with an empty variable list for a given RPTID deletes
that report. Report configurations are not persisted across power cycles; the host must redefine and re-link
reports after each communication session restart as part of its initialisation sequence.

Chapter 1 — Introduction
This document is the authoritative SECS/GEM Interface Control Document (ICD) for the NanoDyne
ETCH-Z500 Reactive Ion Etch System. It defines every aspect of the host-to-equipment communication
interface required to integrate this tool into a factory automation environment under the SEMI E30 Generic
Equipment Model standard. Host software engineers, MES integration teams, and equipment qualification
engineers should use this document as the primary reference for all variable polling, event subscriptions, alarm
handling, remote command sequences, and state machine behaviour.
The ETCH-Z500 is a single-chamber capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) etch system designed for 300 mm
silicon wafer processing. The tool is capable of oxide, nitride, and polysilicon etch processes using CF4/O2/Ar
chemistry. A 13.56 MHz RF generator drives the upper electrode, and a separate bias supply controls the
wafer chuck potential independently. This dual-frequency architecture allows independent control of ion energy
and plasma density, which is critical for achieving the etch selectivity and profile control required at advanced
process nodes.
1.1 Purpose and Scope
This ICD covers the complete set of SECS/GEM objects exposed by the ETCH-Z500 controller: Status
Variables (SVs), Data Variables (DVs), Collection Events (CEIDs), Reports (RPTIDs), Alarms, Remote
Commands (RCMDs), and the equipment state machine. It also documents the HSMS communication
parameters, the VID address space layout, and the GEM compliance posture of the equipment. Process recipe
content, calibration procedures, and hardware maintenance are outside the scope of this document and are
covered in the ETCH-Z500 Process Manual (ND-ETCH-Z500-PM-001).
1.2 Communication Architecture
The ETCH-Z500 uses HSMS-SS (High-Speed Message Services, Single Session) as its transport layer,
operating in Passive mode on TCP port 5011. The equipment listens for an incoming connection from the
factory host; the host is always the TCP client. Once the TCP session is established, the host must initiate the
SECS/GEM session by sending S1F13 (Establish Communications Request). The equipment replies with
S1F14 containing COMMACK=0x00 on success. The host should subscribe to collection events and define its
report structures immediately after a successful S1F14.

Chapter 2 — Status Variables (SV)
Status Variables represent the real-time operating state of the ETCH-Z500 and its subsystems. The host may
read any SV at any time by sending S1F3 (Selected Equipment Status Request) with the desired list of SVIDs;
the equipment replies with S1F4 containing the current values. SVs may also be included in periodic trace
collections configured via S2F23, or delivered automatically inside linked reports when a Collection Event fires
via S6F11.
All SVIDs are read-only unless explicitly marked (R/W) in the table below. Update rates indicate how frequently
the equipment controller refreshes the internal value; the host should not poll faster than the stated rate for
time-sensitive variables such as chamber pressure or RF power. For real-time monitoring of process variables,
the recommended approach is to configure S2F23 trace collection at an appropriate sample interval rather than
issuing repeated S1F3 polls.

Chapter 3 — Data Variables (DV)
Data Variables differ from Status Variables in that their values are event-dependent rather than continuously
updated. A DV holds the value captured at the most recently completed event context — for example,
EtchDepth (DVID 2004) contains the measured etch depth of the last processed wafer and retains that value
until the next wafer completes processing. DVs should not be polled during idle periods; their values are only
meaningful after a relevant event has fired.
The recommended host practice is to receive DVs through linked reports: configure the desired DVIDs into a
report using S2F33, link that report to the relevant Collection Event using S2F35, and enable event reporting
using S2F37. The equipment will then automatically push the correct post-process values in the S6F11 Event
Report Send at exactly the moment they become valid.
DVs 2001–2009 represent process identity and outcome variables. DVs 2010–2012 capture the recipe target
setpoints that were active at process start, providing full traceability of what was commanded versus what was
measured.

Chapter 4 — Collection Events (CEID)
Collection Events are named milestones in the equipment's process and control lifecycle. When an event
occurs, the equipment sends an S6F11 (Event Report Send) message to the host containing the values of all
variables linked to that event through the active report configuration. The host acknowledges with S6F12.
Event reporting is enabled or disabled per-CEID using S2F37 (Enable/Disable Event Report). All events are
disabled at power-on and must be explicitly enabled by the host after establishing communications. At
minimum, the host should enable ProcessStart (3001), ProcessEnd (3002), WaferLoaded (3006),
WaferUnloaded (3007), and AlarmSet (3008) to support standard lot tracking and alarm management
workflows.
4.1 Process Lifecycle Events (CEID 3001–3005)
CEID
Event Name
Linked VIDs
Trigger Condition
3001
ProcessStart
1001, 1003, 1004, 2001, 2002

Chapter 5 — Alarm Definitions
The ETCH-Z500 alarm system continuously monitors critical process and safety parameters. When an alarm
condition is detected, the equipment immediately sends an S5F1 (Alarm Report Send) message containing the
Alarm ID, alarm text, and a set/clear flag. Simultaneously, an AlarmSet Collection Event (CEID 3008) fires,
delivering the linked system status report to the host.
Alarms are classified into two severity levels. Critical alarms represent conditions that pose a risk to personnel
safety, equipment integrity, or wafer integrity. On a critical alarm the equipment immediately aborts any active
process, cuts RF power, and transitions to the FAULT state. The tool cannot resume operation until the alarm is
acknowledged, the root cause resolved, and a RESET_FAULT RCMD is issued by the host. Warning alarms
indicate degraded conditions that do not immediately threaten safety but may affect process quality if
unaddressed. They are logged and reported without aborting the process, unless they persist beyond a defined
tolerance window.

5.3 Alarm Response Procedures
The table below summarises recommended host-side and operator responses. Detailed step-by-step recovery
procedures are in the ETCH-Z500 Process Manual (ND-ETCH-Z500-PM-001).
Alarm
Immediate Host Action
Recovery Steps
OverPressure
Send ABORT_PROCESS RCMD. Do not
vent the chamber.
Check throttle valve position and MFC calibration.
Verify recipe pressure setpoint is within the tool's
operating range. Issue RESET_FAULT once pressure
stabilises below limit.
PlasmaFailure
Log alarm. Poll SVIDs 1005, 1006, 1015 for
diagnostics.
Verify process pressure is within ignition range
(20–200 mTorr). Allow up to 2 automatic ignition
retries. If fault persists after 3 attempts, schedule RF
generator and match network PM.
EMO_Activated
Alert safety officer. Do not attempt remote
reset.
Identify and clear the EMO trigger condition. Perform
full safety walkdown and lockout/tagout clearance.
Physical EMO reset at the tool is required before
issuing RESET_FAULT.
PumpFault
Send ABORT_PROCESS RCMD. Monitor
pump temperature via SVID 1014.
Check pump cooling water supply flow. If bearing or
over-temperature fault, schedule pump replacement.
Do not restart until root cause is confirmed cleared.
RF_MatchFault
Log reflected power trend from SVID 1006.
Inspect match network capacitors and tuning range.
Run the match network self-calibration routine from the
equipment engineering panel. Replace match board
PCB if fault recurs.

Chapter 6 — Remote Commands (RCMD)
Remote Commands allow the factory host to initiate equipment actions using the S2F41 (Host Command
Send) message. The equipment validates each command and replies with S2F42 (Host Command
Acknowledge) containing an HCACK code. HCACK = 0x00 indicates the command was accepted; any
non-zero value indicates rejection, with the reason encoded in the CPACK field of the parameter acknowledge
list.
Commands that affect process state — such as START_PROCESS or ABORT_PROCESS — are only
accepted when the equipment is in ON-LINE REMOTE control state (ControlState SVID 1002 = 5). Commands
sent while the tool is in LOCAL mode will be rejected with HCACK = 0x02 (Cannot perform now). The host
should verify ControlState before issuing process control commands. All command parameters are passed as
CPNAME/CPVAL pairs in the S2F41 body.

Chapter 7 — Equipment State Machine
The ETCH-Z500 process controller implements a deterministic state machine that governs all transitions
between operating modes. Understanding the state machine is essential for writing correct host automation
sequences, because many remote commands are only accepted in specific states. The GEM Control State
(SVID 1002), defined by SEMI E30, is a separate orthogonal state machine that governs the host-equipment
relationship and operates independently of the process state.
The equipment reports its current process state through SystemStatus (SVID 1001). The host can also track
state transitions event-by-event through the Collection Events defined in Chapter 4, which fire automatically as
the tool moves through its process sequence — eliminating the need for the host to poll SystemStatus during a
run.
7.1 State Definitions
State
Description
IDLE
Chamber is at or near atmospheric pressure, at ambient temperature, and fully ready to accept a new
process request. This is the normal resting state between wafer runs.
PUMPING
Vacuum pump-down sequence is in progress. The turbomolecular pump is running and chamber
pressure is decreasing toward the process base pressure target (<5 mTorr). No gas flow or RF
activity.
PURGE
Argon purge gas is flowing through the chamber to displace residual atmospheric contamination
before process gases are introduced. Pressure is controlled at the recipe purge setpoint.
PROCESSING
Active etch step is in progress. Process gases (CF4, O2, Ar) are flowing at recipe setpoints, RF
power is on, plasma is ignited and MATCHED, and the etch timer or endpoint algorithm is running.
COMPLETED
Etch run has finished successfully. The wafer remains on the chuck. The equipment waits for the host
command or robot action to initiate wafer unload.
VENT
Chamber is being vented to atmospheric pressure using a controlled N2 backfill. Entered
automatically after wafer unload to prepare the chamber for the next load cycle.
FAULT
A critical alarm has occurred and the process has been aborted. The chamber is in a safe but
non-operational state. A RESET_FAULT command is required after root cause resolution to return to
IDLE.
MAINTENANCE
Equipment is in maintenance mode following an ENTER_MAINTENANCE command. Process starts
are fully inhibited. Operator has safe access to chamber and gas system.

Chapter 8 — Reports (RPTID)
Reports define named collections of variables that are delivered to the host whenever a linked Collection Event
fires. The host configures reports using S2F33 (Define Report) to specify which variable IDs are grouped under
each RPTID, and uses S2F35 (Link Event Report) to associate each report with one or more CEIDs. This
mechanism ensures the MES receives exactly the data it needs at exactly the right moment — without
continuous polling.
The default report configuration described below is established by the equipment at power-on. The host may
redefine reports at any time using S2F33. Sending S2F33 with an empty variable list for a given RPTID deletes
that report. Report configurations are not persisted across power cycles; the host must redefine and re-link
reports after each communication session restart as part of its initialisation sequence.

Chapter 1 â Introduction
This document is the authoritative SECS/GEM Interface Control Document (ICD) for the NanoDyne
ETCH-Z500 Reactive Ion Etch System. It defines every aspect of the host-to-equipment communication
interface required to integrate this tool into a factory automation environment under the SEMI E30 Generic
Equipment Model standard. Host software engineers, MES integration teams, and equipment qualification
engineers should use this document as the primary reference for all variable polling, event subscriptions, alarm
handling, remote command sequences, and state machine behaviour.
The ETCH-Z500 is a single-chamber capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) etch system designed for 300 mm
silicon wafer processing. The tool is capable of oxide, nitride, and polysilicon etch processes using CF4/O2/Arhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$53623282-3aeb-4808-849b-3928cbefddceh
)}(h
}(hhGh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXÐ␀␀silicon wafer processing. The tool is capable of oxide, nitride, and polysilicon etch processes using CF4/O2/Ar
chemistry. A 13.56 MHz RF generator drives the upper electrode, and a separate bias supply controls the
wafer chuck potential independently. This dual-frequency architecture allows independent control of ion energy
and plasma density, which is critical for achieving the etch selectivity and profile control required at advanced
process nodes.
1.1 Purpose and Scope
This ICD covers the complete set of SECS/GEM objects exposed by the ETCH-Z500 controller: Status
Variables (SVs), Data Variables (DVs), Collection Events (CEIDs), Reports (RPTIDs), Alarms, Remote
Commands (RCMDs), and the equipment state machine. It also documents the HSMS communication
parameters, the VID address space layout, and the GEM compliance posture of the equipment. Process recipe
content, calibration procedures, and hardware maintenance are outside the scope of this document and arehh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$0364cd59-39b7-4717-893e-5fbec7c03b3eh
)}(h
}(hhNh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXê␀␀content, calibration procedures, and hardware maintenance are outside the scope of this document and are
covered in the ETCH-Z500 Process Manual (ND-ETCH-Z500-PM-001).
1.2 Communication Architecture
The ETCH-Z500 uses HSMS-SS (High-Speed Message Services, Single Session) as its transport layer,
operating in Passive mode on TCP port 5011. The equipment listens for an incoming connection from the
factory host; the host is always the TCP client. Once the TCP session is established, the host must initiate the
SECS/GEM session by sending S1F13 (Establish Communications Request). The equipment replies with
S1F14 containing COMMACK=0x00 on success. The host should subscribe to collection events and define its
report structures immediately after a successful S1F14.

Chapter 2 â Status Variables (SV)
Status Variables represent the real-time operating state of the ETCH-Z500 and its subsystems. The host may
read any SV at any time by sending S1F3 (Selected Equipment Status Request) with the desired list of SVIDs;
the equipment replies with S1F4 containing the current values. SVs may also be included in periodic trace
collections configured via S2F23, or delivered automatically inside linked reports when a Collection Event fires
via S6F11.
All SVIDs are read-only unless explicitly marked (R/W) in the table below. Update rates indicate how frequently
the equipment controller refreshes the internal value; the host should not poll faster than the stated rate for
time-sensitive variables such as chamber pressure or RF power. For real-time monitoring of process variables,hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$317734ad-b6d4-4b32-ab59-8e8a262ca0c6h
)}(h
}(hhjh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXà␀␀time-sensitive variables such as chamber pressure or RF power. For real-time monitoring of process variables,
the recommended approach is to configure S2F23 trace collection at an appropriate sample interval rather than
issuing repeated S1F3 polls.

Chapter 3 â Data Variables (DV)
Data Variables differ from Status Variables in that their values are event-dependent rather than continuously
updated. A DV holds the value captured at the most recently completed event context â for example,
EtchDepth (DVID 2004) contains the measured etch depth of the last processed wafer and retains that value
until the next wafer completes processing. DVs should not be polled during idle periods; their values are only
meaningful after a relevant event has fired.
The recommended host practice is to receive DVs through linked reports: configure the desired DVIDs into a
report using S2F33, link that report to the relevant Collection Event using S2F35, and enable event reporting
using S2F37. The equipment will then automatically push the correct post-process values in the S6F11 Eventhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$61d62d24-2a17-4c1e-9a64-5b91c49a51b3h
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXÖ␀␀using S2F37. The equipment will then automatically push the correct post-process values in the S6F11 Event
Report Send at exactly the moment they become valid.
DVs 2001â2009 represent process identity and outcome variables. DVs 2010â2012 capture the recipe target
setpoints that were active at process start, providing full traceability of what was commanded versus what was
measured.

Chapter 4 â Collection Events (CEID)
Collection Events are named milestones in the equipment's process and control lifecycle. When an event
occurs, the equipment sends an S6F11 (Event Report Send) message to the host containing the values of all
variables linked to that event through the active report configuration. The host acknowledges with S6F12.
Event reporting is enabled or disabled per-CEID using S2F37 (Enable/Disable Event Report). All events are
disabled at power-on and must be explicitly enabled by the host after establishing communications. At
minimum, the host should enable ProcessStart (3001), ProcessEnd (3002), WaferLoaded (3006),
WaferUnloaded (3007), and AlarmSet (3008) to support standard lot tracking and alarm management
workflows.

Chapter 5 â Alarm Definitions
The ETCH-Z500 alarm system continuously monitors critical process and safety parameters. When an alarm
condition is detected, the equipment immediately sends an S5F1 (Alarm Report Send) message containing the
Alarm ID, alarm text, and a set/clear flag. Simultaneously, an AlarmSet Collection Event (CEID 3008) fires,
delivering the linked system status report to the host.
Alarms are classified into two severity levels. Critical alarms represent conditions that pose a risk to personnel
safety, equipment integrity, or wafer integrity. On a critical alarm the equipment immediately aborts any active
process, cuts RF power, and transitions to the FAULT state. The tool cannot resume operation until the alarm is
acknowledged, the root cause resolved, and a RESET_FAULT RCMD is issued by the host. Warning alarmshh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$0d4885a2-021a-49b6-9be9-a4a66388250eh
)}(h
}(hhÓh}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhKuhXÜ␀␀acknowledged, the root cause resolved, and a RESET_FAULT RCMD is issued by the host. Warning alarms
indicate degraded conditions that do not immediately threaten safety but may affect process quality if
unaddressed. They are logged and reported without aborting the process, unless they persist beyond a defined
tolerance window.

Chapter 6 â Remote Commands (RCMD)
Remote Commands allow the factory host to initiate equipment actions using the S2F41 (Host Command
Send) message. The equipment validates each command and replies with S2F42 (Host Command
Acknowledge) containing an HCACK code. HCACK = 0x00 indicates the command was accepted; any
non-zero value indicates rejection, with the reason encoded in the CPACK field of the parameter acknowledge
list.
Commands that affect process state â such as START_PROCESS or ABORT_PROCESS â are only
accepted when the equipment is in ON-LINE REMOTE control state (ControlState SVID 1002 = 5). Commands
sent while the tool is in LOCAL mode will be rejected with HCACK = 0x02 (Cannot perform now). The host
should verify ControlState before issuing process control commands. All command parameters are passed ashh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$dafdd0b2-f0ea-48ee-89f0-279889fb6941h
)}(h
}(hj␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhhhK
hK!uhXÍ␀␀should verify ControlState before issuing process control commands. All command parameters are passed as
CPNAME/CPVAL pairs in the S2F41 body.

Chapter 7 â Equipment State Machine
The ETCH-Z500 process controller implements a deterministic state machine that governs all transitions
between operating modes. Understanding the state machine is essential for writing correct host automation
sequences, because many remote commands are only accepted in specific states. The GEM Control State
(SVID 1002), defined by SEMI E30, is a separate orthogonal state machine that governs the host-equipment
relationship and operates independently of the process state.
The equipment reports its current process state through SystemStatus (SVID 1001). The host can also track
state transitions event-by-event through the Collection Events defined in Chapter 4, which fire automatically as
the tool moves through its process sequence â eliminating the need for the host to poll SystemStatus during a
run.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$e6c7c9fd-6f80-405a-bc3a-7bc647adb202h
)}(h
}(hj ␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhK%uhX¨␀␀the tool moves through its process sequence â eliminating the need for the host to poll SystemStatus during a
run.
7.1 State Definitions
State
Description
IDLE
Chamber is at or near atmospheric pressure, at ambient temperature, and fully ready to accept a new
process request. This is the normal resting state between wafer runs.
PUMPING
Vacuum pump-down sequence is in progress. The turbomolecular pump is running and chamber
pressure is decreasing toward the process base pressure target (<5 mTorr). No gas flow or RF
activity.
PURGE
Argon purge gas is flowing through the chamber to displace residual atmospheric contamination
before process gases are introduced. Pressure is controlled at the recipe purge setpoint.
PROCESSING
Active etch step is in progress. Process gases (CF4, O2, Ar) are flowing at recipe setpoints, RF
power is on, plasma is ignited and MATCHED, and the etch timer or endpoint algorithm is running.
COMPLETEDhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$4b09d3d5-efb9-414d-8c69-2bb8bd526d14h
)}(h
}(hj'␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhK&uhX·␀␀power is on, plasma is ignited and MATCHED, and the etch timer or endpoint algorithm is running.
COMPLETED
Etch run has finished successfully. The wafer remains on the chuck. The equipment waits for the host
command or robot action to initiate wafer unload.
VENT
Chamber is being vented to atmospheric pressure using a controlled N2 backfill. Entered
automatically after wafer unload to prepare the chamber for the next load cycle.
FAULT
A critical alarm has occurred and the process has been aborted. The chamber is in a safe but
non-operational state. A RESET_FAULT command is required after root cause resolution to return to
IDLE.
MAINTENANCE
Equipment is in maintenance mode following an ENTER_MAINTENANCE command. Process starts
are fully inhibited. Operator has safe access to chamber and gas system.

Chapter 8 â Reports (RPTID)
Reports define named collections of variables that are delivered to the host whenever a linked Collection Event
fires. The host configures reports using S2F33 (Define Report) to specify which variable IDs are grouped under
each RPTID, and uses S2F35 (Link Event Report) to associate each report with one or more CEIDs. This
mechanism ensures the MES receives exactly the data it needs at exactly the right moment â without
continuous polling.
The default report configuration described below is established by the equipment at power-on. The host may
redefine reports at any time using S2F33. Sending S2F33 with an empty variable list for a given RPTID deletes
that report. Report configurations are not persisted across power cycles; the host must redefine and re-linkhh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$65e7ca17-90b8-4766-802b-7142c7e3f956h
)}(h
}(hjC␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhhhKhK*uhXå␀␀that report. Report configurations are not persisted across power cycles; the host must redefine and re-link
reports after each communication session restart as part of its initialisation sequence.

1.1 Introduction
This document defines the SECS/GEM (SEMI Equipment Communications Standard / Generic Equipment Model)
interface for the semiconductor processing equipment covered herein. It provides a complete description of all
messages, data variables, equipment constants, status variables, collection events, alarms, and operational
scenarios supported by the equipment.
The interface conforms to the SEMI E5 (SECS-II), SEMI E37 (HSMS), and SEMI E30 (GEM) standards. All
equipment communicates with the host system using the message sets described in this manual.
1.2 Compliance
1.2.1 GEM Compliance

1.4 Additional Standards
1.4.1 State Chart Notation
State charts in this document follow the UML statechart notation as referenced in SEMI E30. States are shown as
rounded rectangles, transitions as arrows labeled with triggering events and guard conditions.
1.4.2 System User Interface
The equipment operator interface uses a touch-screen panel. SECS/GEM status is visible from the SECS-GEM
status banner displayed at the top of all major screens. A pop-up dialog is available for operator-initiated control state
changes.
1.4.3 Interface Test Plan and Results
A separate Interface Test Plan document (Form #05-125673B) details all test cases, expected results, and pass/fail

2.1 Configuring Communications Parameters
Communication parameters are configured via the equipment's SECS-GEM setup screen, accessible from the
System Administration menu. Changes take effect after a SECS communication restart.

4.2.1 GemTimeFormat
The equipment uses the GEM time format for all clock-related data. The format is a 16-character ASCII string:
YYYYMMDDHHmmSScc, where YYYY=year, MM=month, DD=day, HH=hour, mm=minute, SS=second,
cc=centisecond.
Example: '20260512143022' = May 12, 2026 at 14:30:22

4.4 User Interface
4.4.1 Banner
The SECS-GEM status banner appears at the top of the equipment's main display screen and shows the current
communication state, control state, and active alarm count. The banner updates in real time.
4.4.2 SECS-GEM Pop Up Dialog Box
A pop-up dialog is displayed when the operator requests a control state change. The dialog shows the current state,
the requested new state, and requires operator confirmation. Conditional buttons appear based on which transitions
are currently valid.hhuhNh(hhhhNub$d6ac1921-a9dc-4be8-8bed-d7975d6fa7a4h

}(hhºh}(hKhhhhhKuhX¬␀␀Chapter 5. Equipment Scenarios
5.1 Establish Communications
The host initiates communication using S1F13. The equipment responds with S1F14 containing the establish
communications acknowledge code (COMMACK).
' Host â Equipment
S1F13 W
<L
 <A ''> ' MDLN (may be empty)
 <A ''> ' SOFTREV (may be empty)
>
.
' Equipment â Host (COMMACK=0: Accepted)
S1F14
<L
 <B 0x00> ' COMMACK = 0 (communication accepted)
 <L> ' MDLN/SOFTREV list (optional)
>
.
5.2 Synchronize
After communications are established, the host synchronizes its understanding of the equipment state by polling
status variables and verifying report/event link configurations.
' Request all status variable values
S1F3 W
<L> ' empty list = request all SVIDs
.
' Equipment response
S1F4
<L
 <A '20260512143022'> ' SVID 2001: CLOCK
 <U1 3> ' SVID 2002: CONTROL_STATE = ON-LINE REMOTE
 <U1 1> ' SVID 2003: E_PROCESSSTATE = IDLE
>
.

5.6 Process Program Management
5.6.1 PPID
Process Program IDs (PPIDs) are ASCII strings up to 80 characters. They uniquely identify a recipe. The equipment
stores up to 200 process programs in non-volatile memory.

5.11.3 Host Accepts ON-LINE
After the equipment transitions to ONLINE-LOCAL, the host may accept remote control using S2F41 withhhuhNh(hhhhNub$4cfbb9c7-341a-4542-a65d-7793156ecdbfh
)}(h

5.11.3 Host Accepts ON-LINE
After the equipment transitions to ONLINE-LOCAL, the host may accept remote control using S2F41 with
RCMD='ENABLE_REMOTE', moving the equipment to ONLINE-REMOTE state.
5.11.4 Host Denies ON-LINE
' S1F18 with ONLACK = 2 (host denied)hhuhNh(hhhhNub$92ca5518-6c0e-4bcf-b1ff-4c099184d687h
)}(h
}(hj␀␀h}(hKhhhhhK$uhXî␀␀S1F18 <B 0x02> .
5.11.5 Operator Sets OFF-LINE
The operator presses the 'OFF-LINE' button on the equipment's local UI. The equipment transitions to OFF-LINE
state and sends an appropriate collection event (CEID 5009).
5.11.6 Operator Sets REMOTE
The operator presses 'REMOTE' on the local UI. The equipment sends a CEID 5009 control state change event and
transitions to ONLINE-REMOTE, enabling host command execution.
5.11.7 Operator Sets LOCAL
The operator presses 'LOCAL' on the local UI. Equipment enters ONLINE-LOCAL state; host remote commands
(S2F41) are rejected with HCACK=4.

6.1 Message Notation
Messages are described using SML (SECS Message Language). Format codes: A=ASCII, B=Binary, BO=Boolean,
U1/U2/U4=Unsigned integer, I1/I2/I4=Signed integer, F4/F8=Float, L=List. The 'W' bit indicates the sender expects a
reply.

A.1 Summary
This appendix provides complete round-trip message sequences for the most common operational scenarios. Each
scenario shows the full SML message exchange between host and equipment.
A.2 Successful Round Trips
' Scenario A-1: Full Communication Establishment and Synchronization
' Step 1 â Are You There
Host â Equip: S1F1 W .
Equip â Host: S1F2 <L <A 'EquipModel-CM1'> <A '2.05'> > .
' Step 2 â Establish Communications
Host â Equip: S1F13 W <L <A ''> <A ''> > .
Equip â Host: S1F14 <L <B 0x00> <L> > .
' Step 3 â Request Time
Host â Equip: S2F17 W .
Equip â Host: S2F18 <A '20260512143022'> .

C.1 Introduction
This appendix provides practical guidance for host-side integration teams deploying the SECS/GEM interface. It
covers common integration patterns, MES interaction sequences, and best practices.
C.2 Material Status and Lot Events
The equipment reports lot and wafer-level events through collection events linked to report definitions. The
recommended integration approach:
1. At communication establishment, the host should re-send all report definitions (S2F33) and event links (S2F35) to
restore the configuration after any equipment restart.
2. The host should track lot state using CEID 5001 (LOT_STARTED) and CEID 5002 (LOT_COMPLETED).
Wafer-level yield tracking should use CEID 5003/5004.
3. Enable spooling for S6F11 and S5F1 to prevent data loss during communication interruptions.

' 1. S1F13 â Establish comms
' 2. S2F17 â Get clock, S2F31 â Sync clockhhuhNh(hhhhNub$d03b9fda-6152-4541-a820-ca17973d4390h
)}(h

C.3 Faults and Recovery
When the equipment detects a fault condition, it sends S5F1 (alarm report) to the host. The host must acknowledge
with S5F2. If no acknowledgment is received within T3, the equipment retries. After maximum retries, the message is
spooled if spooling is configured.
The host should implement the following fault-recovery protocol:
' Fault recovery protocol:
' 1. Host receives S5F1 alarm notification
' 2. Host acknowledges with S5F2 (ACKC5=0)
' 3. Host queries equipment state via S1F3
' 4. If CONTROL_STATE indicates LOCAL, wait for operator actionhhuhNh(hhhhNub$d59a282d-d990-43e1-a9fd-991008217565h
)}(h

' 2. Host acknowledges with S5F2 (ACKC5=0)

' 5. If fault is cleared (S5F1 with ALCD cleared bit), update MES

1.1 Introduction
This document defines the SECS/GEM (SEMI Equipment Communications Standard / Generic Equipment Model)
interface for the semiconductor processing equipment covered herein. It provides a complete description of all
messages, data variables, equipment constants, status variables, collection events, alarms, and operational
scenarios supported by the equipment.
The interface conforms to the SEMI E5 (SECS-II), SEMI E37 (HSMS), and SEMI E30 (GEM) standards. All
equipment communicates with the host system using the message sets described in this manual.

1.4 Additional Standards
1.4.1 State Chart Notation
State charts in this document follow the UML statechart notation as referenced in SEMI E30. States are shown as
rounded rectangles, transitions as arrows labeled with triggering events and guard conditions.
1.4.2 System User Interface
The equipment operator interface uses a touch-screen panel. SECS/GEM status is visible from the SECS-GEM
status banner displayed at the top of all major screens. A pop-up dialog is available for operator-initiated control state
changes.

4.2.1 GemTimeFormat
The equipment uses the GEM time format for all clock-related data. The format is a 16-character ASCII string:
YYYYMMDDHHmmSScc, where YYYY=year, MM=month, DD=day, HH=hour, mm=minute, SS=second,
cc=centisecond.
Example: '20260512143022' = May 12, 2026 at 14:30:22

4.4 User Interface
4.4.1 Banner
The SECS-GEM status banner appears at the top of the equipment's main display screen and shows the current
communication state, control state, and active alarm count. The banner updates in real time.
4.4.2 SECS-GEM Pop Up Dialog Box

the requested new state, and requires operator confirmation. Conditional buttons appear based on which transitions

5.1 Establish Communications
The host initiates communication using S1F13. The equipment responds with S1F14 containing the establish
communications acknowledge code (COMMACK).
' Host â Equipment
S1F13 W
<L
 <A ''> ' MDLN (may be empty)
 <A ''> ' SOFTREV (may be empty)
>
.
' Equipment â Host (COMMACK=0: Accepted)
S1F14
<L
 <B 0x00> ' COMMACK = 0 (communication accepted)
 <L> ' MDLN/SOFTREV list (optional)
>
.
5.2 Synchronize
After communications are established, the host synchronizes its understanding of the equipment state by polling
status variables and verifying report/event link configurations.
' Request all status variable values
S1F3 W
<L> ' empty list = request all SVIDs
.
' Equipment response
S1F4
<L
 <A '20260512143022'> ' SVID 2001: CLOCK
 <U1 3> ' SVID 2002: CONTROL_STATE = ON-LINE REMOTE
 <U1 1> ' SVID 2003: E_PROCESSSTATE = IDLE
>
.

5.6 Process Program Management
5.6.1 PPID
Process Program IDs (PPIDs) are ASCII strings up to 80 characters. They uniquely identify a recipe. The equipment
stores up to 200 process programs in non-volatile memory.

5.11.4 Host Denies ON-LINE
' S1F18 with ONLACK = 2 (host denied)jè␀␀h	uhNh(jÝ␀␀jæ␀␀jÞ␀␀hNub$0ab8a900-8cf8-4dc7-b87c-abcf334d2b69h

5.11.5 Operator Sets OFF-LINE
The operator presses the 'OFF-LINE' button on the equipment's local UI. The equipment transitions to OFF-LINE
state and sends an appropriate collection event (CEID 5009).
5.11.6 Operator Sets REMOTE
The operator presses 'REMOTE' on the local UI. The equipment sends a CEID 5009 control state change event and
transitions to ONLINE-REMOTE, enabling host command execution.
5.11.7 Operator Sets LOCAL
The operator presses 'LOCAL' on the local UI. Equipment enters ONLINE-LOCAL state; host remote commands
(S2F41) are rejected with HCACK=4.

6.1 Message Notation
Messages are described using SML (SECS Message Language). Format codes: A=ASCII, B=Binary, BO=Boolean,
U1/U2/U4=Unsigned integer, I1/I2/I4=Signed integer, F4/F8=Float, L=List. The 'W' bit indicates the sender expects a
reply.

C.1 Introduction
This appendix provides practical guidance for host-side integration teams deploying the SECS/GEM interface. It
covers common integration patterns, MES interaction sequences, and best practices.
C.2 Material Status and Lot Events
The equipment reports lot and wafer-level events through collection events linked to report definitions. The
recommended integration approach:
1. At communication establishment, the host should re-send all report definitions (S2F33) and event links (S2F35) to
restore the configuration after any equipment restart.
2. The host should track lot state using CEID 5001 (LOT_STARTED) and CEID 5002 (LOT_COMPLETED).
Wafer-level yield tracking should use CEID 5003/5004.
3. Enable spooling for S6F11 and S5F1 to prevent data loss during communication interruptions.
' Recommended startup sequence for MES integration:
' 1. S1F13 â Establish comms
' 2. S2F17 â Get clock, S2F31 â Sync clockjè␀␀h	uhNh(jÝ␀␀jæ␀␀jÞ␀␀hNub$f41d93f6-0290-495d-b0ff-c59abeb52a96h
)}(h
}(jÝ␀␀j␀␀jÞ␀␀}(jà␀␀Kjá␀␀jâ␀␀jã␀␀jä␀␀jå␀␀K=ujæ␀␀Xñ␀␀' Recommended startup sequence for MES integration:
' 1. S1F13 â Establish comms
' 2. S2F17 â Get clock, S2F31 â Sync clock
' 3. S1F3 â Get all status variables to seed MES state
' 4. S2F33 â Re-define all required reports
' 5. S2F35 â Re-link all CEID-RPTID associations
' 6. S2F37 â Enable all required CEIDs
' 7. S2F43 â Configure spooling for S6F11 and S5F1
' 8. S5F5 â Request full alarm list to sync alarm state
C.3 Faults and Recovery
When the equipment detects a fault condition, it sends S5F1 (alarm report) to the host. The host must acknowledge
with S5F2. If no acknowledgment is received within T3, the equipment retries. After maximum retries, the message is
spooled if spooling is configured.
The host should implement the following fault-recovery protocol:
' Fault recovery protocol:
' 1. Host receives S5F1 alarm notification
' 2. Host acknowledges with S5F2 (ACKC5=0)
' 3. Host queries equipment state via S1F3
' 4. If CONTROL_STATE indicates LOCAL, wait for operator actionjè␀␀h	uhNh(jÝ␀␀jæ␀␀jÞ␀␀hNub$9c90d121-bac7-4b0d-8461-2f2139472d7ah
)}(h
}(jÝ␀␀j␀␀jÞ␀␀}(jà␀␀Kjá␀␀jâ␀␀jã␀␀jä␀␀jå␀␀K>ujæ␀␀XÃ␀␀' 1. Host receives S5F1 alarm notification
' 2. Host acknowledges with S5F2 (ACKC5=0)
' 3. Host queries equipment state via S1F3
' 4. If CONTROL_STATE indicates LOCAL, wait for operator action
' 5. If fault is cleared (S5F1 with ALCD cleared bit), update MES
' 6. For process abort: host may send S2F41 ABORT command
' 7. Equipment sends CEID 5010 when process state changes post-fault

Chapter 1 — Introduction
1.1 Purpose and Scope
This document defines the SECS/GEM host-to-equipment interface for the CVD-F800 Dual-Chamber Thermal
Chemical Vapor Deposition system. It specifies all Status Variables (SV), Data Variables (DV), Collection Events
(CEID), Alarms, Remote Commands (RCMD), Reports (RPTID), and state machine transitions required for full GEM
compliance under SEMI E30. Host systems integrating this equipment shall use this document as the authoritative
reference for all message exchanges, variable polling, event subscriptions, and alarm management.
1.2 GEM Compliance Summary
The CVD-F800 implements the complete set of required and selected optional GEM capabilities as listed below. All
SEMI E30 mandatory capabilities are implemented.

Chapter 2 — Equipment Configuration
2.1 Physical and Electrical Setup
The CVD-F800 connects to the host factory network via a dedicated 1 Gbps Ethernet interface. The equipment
controller runs an embedded Linux OS and exposes the SECS/GEM interface through a single HSMS-SS passive
listener. All communication is on VLAN 30 (Equipment Network). A separate service port (VLAN 50) is reserved for
maintenance and is not part of the GEM interface.

2.3 Device Configuration
The CVD-F800 is configured as a single logical device (DeviceID = 1). Both process chambers (Chamber A and
Chamber B) share one SECS/GEM device ID. Chamber-specific variables are differentiated by VID range as follows:

3.2 Dual-Chamber Architecture
The CVD-F800 employs two independently controlled process chambers sharing a common wafer handling robot and
gas delivery manifold. Each chamber has its own temperature controller (5-zone heater stack), pressure controller, RF
generator, and gas injection ring. Chambers may run different recipes simultaneously. The shared robot services both
chambers and reports its status through the global SV range (VID 1000–1099). Chamber-specific interlocks ensure
that a fault in Chamber A does not abort an active process in Chamber B unless a shared resource (gas manifold,
exhaust) is affected.

CVD-F800 SECS/GEM Interface Specification  |  Revision C  |  FabTech Systems Inc.

Chapter 4 — Status Variables (SV)
Status Variables are real-time equipment parameters that the host may read at any time using S1F3/F4 (request
selected equipment status) or S1F5/F6 (request formatted status). All SVIDs are read-only unless noted otherwise.
Values are refreshed by the equipment controller at the update rates shown.

Chapter 5 — Data Variables (DV)
Data Variables represent process parameters, recipe settings, and metrology results. They are typically read after a
process event (e.g., at ProcessEnd) using S6F1/F2 or as part of a linked report delivered with S6F11. Unlike Status
Variables, DVs may have undefined values outside of an active process step.

Chapter 6 — Collection Events (CEID)
Collection Events are named points in the equipment's process or control flow at which the equipment notifies the host
and delivers a set of associated variable values. Events are reported via S6F11 (Event Report Send). The host
enables event reporting using S2F37 (Enable/Disable Event Report).

Chapter 7 — Reports (RPTID)
Reports define named collections of variables that are delivered to the host when a linked Collection Event fires. The
host configures report-event links using S2F33 (Define Report) and S2F35 (Link Event Report). Default links are
established at equipment startup and persist until the host redefines them.

Chapter 8 — Alarm Definitions
Alarms are abnormal equipment conditions reported to the host via S5F1 (Alarm Report Send). Critical alarms result in
immediate process abort. Warning alarms are logged and reported but do not abort the process unless the condition
persists beyond the defined tolerance window. All alarms may be individually enabled or disabled by the host using
S5F3.

8.3 Alarm Response Procedures
The following table summarises recommended host-side responses to critical alarms. Detailed step-by-step
procedures are provided in Appendix C.
 Alarm
 Immediate Response
 Recovery Action
ChamberA/B_OverTemp
erature
Send ABORT_PROCESS RCMD.
Do not open chamber.
Wait for cool-down. Check thermocouple
wiring. Inspect heater element.
PlasmaFailure
Log alarm, check RF match network
status.
Retry ignition. If 3 consecutive failures:
schedule RF generator PM.
GasLeak / H2_Leak
Evacuate zone. Activate facility gas
shutoff.
Do not re-enter until leak confirmed cleared by
facilities team.
EMO_Activated
All processes halt automatically.
Identify EMO trigger. Clear condition. Perform
safety check before restart.
Robot_CollisionFault
Send robot to HOME position.
Inspect for obstruction. Check wafer presence
sensors.

Chapter 9 — Remote Commands (RCMD)
Remote Commands allow the host to initiate equipment actions using S2F41 (Host Command Send). The equipment
acknowledges each command with S2F42. Commands that affect process state will generate corresponding
Collection Events upon completion. Parameters are passed as a list of CPNAME/CPVAL pairs in the S2F41 body.

Chapter 10 — Equipment State Machine
10.1 State Definitions
Each process chamber maintains an independent sub-state. The global equipment state is the composite of both
chambers. The GEM Control State (SV 1002) is a separate orthogonal state machine defined by SEMI E30.
 State
 Applies To
 Description
IDLE
 Chamber A/B
 Chamber is at atmospheric pressure, at ambient temperature, and ready to
 accept a new process request.
PUMPING
 Chamber A/B
 Vacuum pump-down in progress. Pressure is decreasing towards base vacuum.
PURGE
 Chamber A/B
 N2 purge gas flowing. Chamber is being cleaned of residual gases prior to
 process.
RAMP
 Chamber A/B
 Heaters ramping temperature towards the process setpoint at the programmed
 ramp rate.
SOAK
 Chamber A/B
 Temperature within tolerance of setpoint. Waiting for thermal stabilisation period
 to expire.
DEPOSIT
 Chamber A/B
Active deposition step. Process gases flowing, RF on (for PECVD recipes), wafer
 being processed.
COOL
 Chamber A/B
 Heaters off or set to low temperature. Chamber cooling before wafer unload.
VENT
 Chamber A/B
 N2 vent in progress. Pressure rising to atmospheric for safe wafer unload.
COMPLETED
 Chamber A/B
 Process run finished successfully. Wafer ready for unload by robot.
FAULT
 Chamber A/B
 A critical alarm has stopped the process. Chamber not available until fault is
 cleared.
MAINTENANCE
 Global
 Equipment-wide maintenance mode. Both chambers inhibited.

Appendix C — Alarm Response Procedures (Detailed)
ALID 4001 / 4006 — Chamber Over-Temperature
1. Send ABORT_PROCESS RCMD immediately for the affected chamber.
2. Do NOT open the chamber door. Allow natural cool-down with N2 flowing.
3. Monitor SVIDs 1101–1105 (or 1201–1205) until all zones <200 degC.
4. Check thermocouple continuity on the faulted zone.
5. Inspect heater power relay and zone controller for faults.
6. If hardware confirmed healthy, send RESET_FAULT RCMD with FAULT_CODE=0x01.
7. If fault recurs within 3 cycles, schedule preventive maintenance.
ALID 4003 / 4008 — Plasma Failure
1. Verify process gas flows are within specification (check SVIDs 1301–1308).
2. Check RF generator fault code (accessible via S10 terminal message).
3. Verify chamber pressure is within ignition range (50–500 mTorr).
4. Send START_PROCESS RCMD again (up to 2 automatic retries are allowed).
5. If 3 consecutive ignition failures, lock out the chamber and call RF maintenance.
ALID 4005 / 4010 — Gas Leak Detected
1. Immediately activate facility gas shutoff valve for the affected gas species.
2. Evacuate all personnel from the gas cabinet bay.
3. Notify facility safety officer before re-entry.
4. Do not send RESET_FAULT until leak source is confirmed cleared by leak detection.
5. Document event in facility safety log.
ALID 4013 — EMO Activated
1. Identify the cause of the EMO activation before approaching equipment.
2. All in-progress processes are aborted. Wafers in chambers may be at risk.
3. Follow lockout/tagout procedure before any physical inspection.
4. Once safe, perform full equipment integrity check before resetting EMO.
5. Issue RESET_FAULT after safety check is documented and signed off.

CVD-F800 SECS/GEM Interface Specification  |  Revision C  |  FabTech Systems Inc.

Chapter 1. Introduction 
 
1.1 Introduction 
This document describes the SECS/GEM interface implementation for the Plasma Etching System, 
Model ETCH-PRO-X100, as deployed in the ETCH-PRO-X100 project at Fab-Alpha, Bay 3. It 
provides the information necessary for a host system (MES/CIM) to establish communication with 
the equipment, collect process data, respond to alarms, and control the equipment in accordance 
with SEMI standards. 
This manual is intended for use by equipment engineers, MES integration teams, and automation 
software developers who are responsible for qualifying and deploying the SECS/GEM interface. 
 
1.2 Compliance 
1.2.1 GEM Compliance 
The ETCH-PRO-X100 implements the GEM (Generic Equipment Model) interface as defined in 
SEMI E30. The following table lists the GEM compliance statements applicable to this equipment.

1.4.2 System User Interface 
The ETCH-PRO-X100 equipment software provides a SECS-GEM pop-up dialog accessible from 
the equipment banner. This dialog allows the operator to view current communication state, 
manually set the equipment ONLINE/OFFLINE, and acknowledge terminal messages from the host. 
 
1.4.3 Interface Test Plan and Results 
A formal GEM compliance test must be completed before production release. The test plan covers 
all required GEM capabilities listed in Section 1.2.1. Test results shall be documented and signed 
off by the equipment engineer and MES integration lead. Refer to the Interface Test Plan document 
(Form #ITP-EQP5000-001) for test procedures and pass/fail criteria.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$6c1b8e2e-cce5-4978-a904-be2650f53e65h

Chapter 2. Equipment Configuration Procedure 
 
This chapter describes how to configure the communication parameters of the ETCH-PRO-X100 for 
use with a host system. All configuration is performed through the equipment software interface. 
 
2.1 Configuring Communications Parameters 
The ETCH-PRO-X100 uses HSMS (SEMI E37) as its primary communication protocol. SECS-1 
(RS-232 serial) is not supported on this model. Before the host can establish a session, the HSMS 
port and device parameters must be configured on the equipment side. 
 
2.1.1 Defining an HSMS Port 
Navigate to the SECS/GEM configuration screen in the equipment software and enter the following 
parameters to define the HSMS connection.

Chapter 4. Equipment Scenarios 
 
This chapter describes the operational scenarios that define how the host and the ETCH-PRO-
X100 interact. Each scenario presents the sequence of messages exchanged and the expected 
behavior of both parties. 
 
4.1 Establish Communications 
Before any data collection or control activity can occur, the host must establish a communication 
session with the equipment. The ETCH-PRO-X100 operates in HSMS Passive mode; the host 
initiates the TCP connection.

4.5 Equipment Constants 
Equipment Constants (ECs) are configurable parameters that affect equipment behavior. The host 
can read and write ECs using S2F13/S2F15. The ETCH-PRO-X100 supports 30 configurable 
equipment constants (ECID 1001-1030). Key constants include: MaxProcessTimeSec (1001), 
ChamberMaxTempC (1003), RFPowerMaxWatt (1012), GasFlowMaxSccm (1011), and 
SimulationModeEnable (1030).

4.11.5 Operator Sets OFF-LINE 
The equipment operator can place the equipment in OFF-LINE state directly from the equipment

4.11.6 Operator Sets REMOTE 
When the operator sets the equipment to REMOTE control, the equipment is fully controllable by 
the host via RCMD (S2F41). Local operator input is restricted to safety functions only.

When the operator sets the equipment to LOCAL control, host RCMD commands are rejected. The

control state).

Chapter 5. Message Detail 
 
This chapter provides detailed specifications for each SECS-II message supported by the ETCH-
PRO-X100. Messages are presented in Stream/Function order. SML notation is used to describe 
message structure. 
 
5.1 Message Notation 
Messages in this chapter use SECS Message Language (SML) notation. The following conventions 
apply: 
 
Convention 
Meaning 
L[n] 
List of n items 
L[] 
Empty list 
A[n] 
ASCII string of length n 
U2 
2-byte unsigned integer 
U4 
4-byte unsigned integer 
I2 
2-byte signed integer 
F4 
4-byte IEEE floating point 
BOOLEAN 
Single boolean byte 
B[n] 
Binary data of length n 
<name> 
Named data item â see SEMI E5 for formal definition 
{...} 
Optional element

 > 
 > .

Chapter 6. Alarms 
 
The ETCH-PRO-X100 defines the following alarm conditions. All alarms are reported via S5F1 
when enabled. The host can enable or disable individual alarms using S5F3. 
Alarm codes use bit 7 of the ALCD byte to indicate alarm state: bit 7 = 1 means alarm is SET; bit 7 
= 0 means alarm is CLEARED. The lower 7 bits indicate whether the alarm is currently enabled (bit 
0 = 1 enabled).

6.1 Alarm Recovery Procedures 
ChamberOverheat (1001) and VacuumPressureTooHigh (1003) â Critical 
These alarms place the equipment in the ERROR state. The equipment halts all process activity 
immediately. The host receives S5F1 with ALCD bit 7 set. The host must: 
1. Acknowledge the alarm with S5F2. 
2. Investigate the root cause via equipment diagnostics. 
3. Once the condition is resolved, send S2F41 with RCMD='RESET' to return the equipment to 
IDLE state. 
4. The equipment will send S5F1 with ALCD bit 7 clear when the alarm condition is resolved. 
 
RobotNotHomed (1002) and VacuumPumpFailure (1004) â Warning 
These alarms do not halt the process. The host receives S5F1 and should acknowledge with S5F2. 
The host may choose to abort the process using S2F41 RCMD='STOP' or allow it to continue. The 
alarm clears automatically when the condition returns to normal.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$280196c6-a706-4dc0-a1f9-a0d1da03058ch

Appendix B. Application Notes 
 
B.1 Introduction 
This appendix provides guidance on implementing common automation scenarios for the ETCH-
PRO-X100. These notes are based on known integration patterns and are intended to supplement 
the message specifications in Chapter 5. 
 
B.2 Material Status and Lot Events 
The ETCH-PRO-X100 supports lot-level event tracking through collection events 5200 
(CarrierLoaded) and 5201 (CarrierUnloaded). The host should link the DV 3002 (WaferID) to a 
report on these events to maintain material traceability. 
Recommended practice: the host should log 5001 (ProcessStarted) with the active RecipeID (3001) 
and 5002 (ProcessCompleted) with EtchTime (3007) and EtchDepth (3016) as the minimum lot 
record for each wafer. 
For multi-wafer lots, the host should correlate WaferLoaded/WaferUnloaded events with the lothh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$f0184b39-da88-442d-a415-0a7e4b1542ebh
)}(h
}(hjÖ␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhhhK#hK?uhX®␀␀record for each wafer. 
For multi-wafer lots, the host should correlate WaferLoaded/WaferUnloaded events with the lot 
traveler to ensure each wafer's process history is captured individually. 
 
B.3 Faults and Recovery 
The ETCH-PRO-X100 state machine has the following recovery paths after a fault condition: 
PROCESSING â ERROR (triggered by 1003 VacuumPressureTooHigh or 1001 
ChamberOverheat) 
ERROR â IDLE (triggered by RCMD='RESET' from host or operator manual reset) 
The host should implement an alarm handler that: (1) acknowledges the S5F1, (2) logs the alarm 
with timestamp and CEID context, (3) optionally pages the operator, and (4) waits for the operator 
to clear the physical condition before sending RESET. 
If the RESET command is sent before the physical alarm condition is resolved, the equipment will 
reject it with HCACK=2 (cannot perform now). The host should implement a retry loop with a 
configurable timeout.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nub$727ef439-2d9d-415b-8471-e69e2011702dh
)}(h
}(hjÝ␀␀h}(hKhhhhhhhhhK#hK@uhXm␀␀reject it with HCACK=2 (cannot perform now). The host should implement a retry loop with a 
configurable timeout. 
For Warning-class alarms (1002, 1004), the host may choose to allow the process to continue or 
abort using STOP. The decision should be based on the magnitude and duration of the deviation, 
as specified in the process specification for each recipe.hh	uh Nh!(hhhh#Nubusb}(K␀hKh$Kh+Kh2Kh9Kh@KhGKhNKhUK	h\K

Chapter 1 â Introduction
1.1 Purpose and Scope
This manual describes the operation, architecture, and SECS/GEM host interface of the IMP-HE2000 High-Energy
Medium-Current Ion Implanter manufactured by PrecisionBeam Technologies. It covers equipment subsystems,
process workflows, state machine behaviour, alarm handling, and remote command capabilities. For all tabular data â
including variable IDs, event codes, alarm definitions, report structures, and state transitions â refer to the companion
workbook: IMP_HE2000_Variable_Tables.xlsx.
1.2 How to Use This Manual
This manual is the prose companion to the Variable Tables workbook. The manual explains HOW the equipment
works and WHY variables/events/alarms exist. The workbook provides the WHAT â exact IDs, types, ranges, and
linkages. Together they form the complete SECS/GEM Interface Control Document (ICD).
1.3 Companion Documentshh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$ebc8dd8c-e78e-4f6b-bcfb-fda445b01d99h

1.4 Terminology and Abbreviations
AMU (Atomic Mass Unit): The unit of measurement used to specify the mass of ions. It is critical in mass
spectrometry and ion beam mass analysis to ensure only the desired dopant species is selected and accelerated
toward the wafer.
AsHâ  (Arsine): A toxic process gas used as a precursor to supply Arsenic (As) ions for n-type doping of silicon
substrates.

CEID (Collection Event ID): A unique numeric identifier representing an equipment event that the host can subscribe
to, such as a process step starting, wafer loading, or status transition.
DV / DVID (Data Variable / Data Variable ID): A dynamic variable whose value is updated only during or upon
completion of specific events (e.g., post-implant wafer results).
EC (Equipment Constant): A user-configurable setpoint or operational parameter stored in the equipment controller
that governs local tool behaviour and can be modified by the host.
GEM (Generic Equipment Model): The SEMI E30 standard defining a generic model for communications and control
of manufacturing equipment by a host computer in a semiconductor fab.

HSMS (High-Speed Message Services): The SEMI E37 standard defining the TCP/IP-based transport layer protocol
used to transmit SECS-II messages between the equipment and the host.
keV (kilo-electron-Volt): A unit of energy representing the kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerating through a
potential difference of one thousand volts. It is the standard unit for specifying ion beam energy.

Chapter 2 â Equipment Overview
2.1 System Architecture
The PrecisionBeam IMP-HE2000 is a high-energy, medium-current ion implanter designed specifically for 300 mm
silicon wafer processing in modern semiconductor fabs. The system consists of seven primary hardware subsystems:
the Ion Source, the Beamline, the End Station, the Wafer Handler, the Vacuum System, the High-Voltage System, and
the central Control System. All subsystems interface directly with the equipment controller, which hosts the
SECS/GEM software stack and manages the factory automation link over HSMS-SS.
2.2 Ion Source Subsystem
The ion source is a Freeman-type hot cathode source designed for high plasma stability. Precursor gases (BFâ , PHâ ,
AsHâ , or Ar for setup) are introduced into the arc chamber via mass flow controllers. A tungsten filament is heated tohh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$fbc438fb-ddef-46f2-afbc-4a1e51f2f706h
)}(h
}(hhgh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhX␀␀AsHâ , or Ar for setup) are introduced into the arc chamber via mass flow controllers. A tungsten filament is heated to
thermionic emission temperatures, and an electrical discharge (arc voltage) ignites a dense plasma inside the
chamber. An extraction electrode assembly pulls positive ions from the plasma aperture, forming a preliminary ion
beam. Real-time parameters include arc current, filament current, extraction voltage, and source gas pressure. The
filament and arc chamber have finite lifetimes and require periodic maintenance, tracked by local timers.
2.3 Beamline Subsystem
The beamline collimates, refines, and accelerates the extracted ion beam. An analyzer magnet acts as a mass
spectrometer, bending the ion path through a 90-degree arc. Since mass deflection is proportional to charge, only the
desired dopant species (e.g., Boron-11) passes through the resolving aperture, filtering out contaminants andhh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$85498de3-8a6f-4df9-9448-7adff245f61dh
)}(h
}(hhnh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhXå␀␀desired dopant species (e.g., Boron-11) passes through the resolving aperture, filtering out contaminants and
unwanted carrier species. The filtered beam is then accelerated or decelerated in the high-voltage column to match
recipe requirements. Electrostatic scan plates deflect the beam at high frequencies to create a uniform scanning
ribbon beam. Multi-point Faraday cups measure the beam current to ensure stability and parallelism.
2.4 End Station Subsystem
The end station houses the process chamber where wafers undergo ion implantation under high vacuum. A wafer is
held on an electrostatic chuck (platen) that provides Helium backside cooling to maintain wafer temperature below
critical photoresist degradation levels (typically < 120Â°C). The platen tilt and twist mechanisms position the wafer
relative to the incoming beam, avoiding crystal channeling. A Faraday cup array behind the platen measures the
actual dose in real-time, halting the implant when the target dose is achieved.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$68943ba4-575d-400b-984f-1f62f4472c46h
)}(h
}(hhuh}(hKhhhhhhhK
uhXæ␀␀relative to the incoming beam, avoiding crystal channeling. A Faraday cup array behind the platen measures the
actual dose in real-time, halting the implant when the target dose is achieved.
2.5 Wafer Handling Subsystem
The wafer handler manages wafer transfer between atmospheric and vacuum environments. It features two FOUP
load ports, an atmospheric transfer robot with a slot-mapping sensor, an optical notch pre-aligner, a vacuum load lock
chamber, and a vacuum transfer arm. Wafers are transferred individually to the process platen, maintaining high
vacuum in the process chamber during lot processing.
2.6 Vacuum System
High-vacuum integrity is vital to prevent ion beam scattering and wafer contamination. The beamline is evacuated by
dual turbomolecular pumps backed by dry scroll pumps. The end station process chamber uses a cryogenic pump for
ultra-high vacuum (~10â â  Torr). Gate valves isolate the subsystems, and vacuum gauges continuously monitor
pressures across all chambers.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$6ef192c7-bff9-448d-9570-abb16dac338ah
)}(h
}(hh|h}(hKhhhhhhhKuhX␀␀ultra-high vacuum (~10â â  Torr). Gate valves isolate the subsystems, and vacuum gauges continuously monitor
pressures across all chambers.
2.7 High-Voltage System
The high-voltage system provides acceleration potentials up to 200 kV inside an insulated terminal. Terminal voltage,
extraction voltage, and suppression power supplies are managed by a dedicated HV controller. Hardwired interlocks
disable high-voltage generation if vacuum thresholds are violated or access panel switches are tripped.
2.8 Safety Systems and Interlockshh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$7a1b6a97-95a9-4be9-a26c-8d72586ca8afh
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhXö␀␀IMP-HE2000 SECS/GEM User Manual | Revision A | PrecisionBeam Technologies
Page 7
Personnel and equipment safety are maintained through a distributed interlock system. The interlock loop monitors
toxic gas detectors (for Arsine and Phosphine leaks), radiation levels (X-ray monitoring near the high-voltage column),
vacuum pressures, cooling water flow, and the Emergency Master Off (EMO) buttons. If any safety threshold is
exceeded, the beam shutter is immediately closed, and high voltage is tripped.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$beab7616-42b5-4347-94ba-ba3a81983589h

Chapter 3 â Communication Configuration
3.1 HSMS Communication Parameters
The HSMS interface on the IMP-HE2000 operates in Passive mode, meaning the tool listens for an incoming
connection from the factory host. The default TCP port is 5020. Standard timeout parameters (T3, T5, T6, T7, and T8)
are set to SEMI E37 defaults. These values can be modified locally on the tool's engineering panel or remotely via
SECS-II messages.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'HSMS Parameters', for the complete list of network
settings, IP addresses, port configuration, and timeout limits.
3.2 Device Configuration and VID Ranges
The IMP-HE2000 is represented as a single logical SECS-II device with DeviceID = 1. To organize the large number of

Chapter 4 â Status Variables (SV) â Description
Status Variables (SVs) represent continuously updated, real-time parameters monitored by the IMP-HE2000 control
computer. The host can poll these variables at any time using S1F3/F4 messages or include them in periodic trace
definitions (S2F23) or linked event reports (S2F35).
4.1 Global System Variables
Global variables track tool-wide states, GEM control states, and system-wide safety interlocks. These variables help
the host verify the current operating mode (e.g., IDLE, IMPLANTING) and ensure safety conditions are met before
starting a run.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Global System', for the complete list of global
variables, including SystemStatus, ControlState, and EMOStatus.
4.2 Ion Source Variables
Ion source variables monitor the health and discharge characteristics of the Freeman plasma source. Parametershh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$c0d387a7-a561-4162-96ee-88a1ac88d063h
)}(h
}(hhh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhX␀␀variables, including SystemStatus, ControlState, and EMOStatus.
4.2 Ion Source Variables
Ion source variables monitor the health and discharge characteristics of the Freeman plasma source. Parameters
include arc current, filament current, filament voltage, extraction voltage, gas flow rate, and gas species. These values
are refreshed every 500 ms.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Ion Source', for all source-related SVs.
4.3 Beamline Variables
Beamline variables monitor ion beam transport and beam qualities, such as mass analyzer coil current, beam energy,
resolved Faraday cup current, electrostatic scan frequencies, spot sizes, and beam parallelism. These are critical to
verify that the ion beam is properly tuned and aligned before implanting the wafer.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Beamline', for the beamline variables list.

4.4 End Station Variables
End station variables track process chamber parameters during implantation, including platen tilt/twist angles, wafer
clamp status, backside helium cooling flow, and real-time dose accumulation. Fast updates (200 ms) are provided for
critical dose and beam current parameters.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - End Station', for end station SV details.
4.5 Wafer Handler Variables
Wafer handler variables track the robot state, robot end-effector positions, load lock chamber pressure, load lock
pump/vent states, pre-aligner notch angle, and FOUP wafer mapping counts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'SV - Wafer Handler', for handling SVs.

Chapter 5 â Data Variables (DV) â Description
Data Variables (DVs) differ from Status Variables in that their values are event-dependent. They represent process
setup targets and post-process results (such as lot ID, recipe settings, measured dose, uniformity, and particle
counts). These values are updated at specific event triggers (like ImplantStart and ImplantEnd) and are typically read
by the host inside linked reports rather than polled during idle periods.
5.1 Recipe and Implant Target Variables
These variables capture the target process parameters defined in the active recipe, including the Target Species,
Target Energy, Target Dose, and Target Platen Tilt/Twist angles. They are updated when a recipe is loaded or an
implant run starts.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Recipe and Implant Targets', for recipe DVs.

Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Recipe and Implant Targets', for recipe DVs.
5.2 Process Result and Metrology Variables
Post-process variables contain metrology and quality assurance results for the most recently processed wafer, such
as actual dose delivered, measured dose uniformity, average beam current, implant duration, maximum wafer
temperature, ellipsometry results, and the process outcome (PASS/FAIL). These variables are updated when the
wafer processing ends or is aborted.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'DV - Process Results', for results and metrology DVs.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$e1e8e4b9-613f-4b2c-a054-ca3d73b8b964h

Chapter 6 â Collection Events (CEID) â Description
Collection Events (CEIDs) represent milestones in the equipment's physical and logical workflow. When an event
occurs, the equipment sends an S6F11 Event Report message containing linked reports to the host. The host can
dynamically enable or disable reporting for individual event IDs using the S2F37 message.
6.1 Implant Lifecycle Events
Implant lifecycle events track progress during wafer processing. The primary lifecycle events are ImplantStart,
ImplantEnd, and ImplantAbort. These events allow the host to track processing times and receive detailed
post-implant results immediately after a wafer is processed.
6.2 Beam Tuning Events
Beam tuning events notify the host of beam preparation progress. They include BeamTuneStart, BeamTuneComplete,
BeamLost, SourceIgnition, SourceExtinguish, and SourceFault. These events help the host monitor source stabilityhh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$3a9f6c17-5004-45fb-968f-558f12ff171bh
)}(h
}(hhÐh}(hKhhhhhhhKuhXÀ␀␀BeamLost, SourceIgnition, SourceExtinguish, and SourceFault. These events help the host monitor source stability
and track beam setup durations.
6.3 Wafer Handling Events
Handling events track wafer and FOUP movements. Key events include WaferLoaded_EndStation,
WaferUnloaded_EndStation, WaferPrealigned, FOUPLoaded_Port1/2, FOUPUnloaded_Port1/2,
LoadLockPumpDown, LoadLockVacuumReached, and LoadLockVent. These events allow tracking of wafer locations
within the tool.
6.4 System and Maintenance Events
System events track state changes and maintenance intervals. They include ControlStateChange, RecipeLoaded,
RecipeDeleted, MaintenanceModeEntered/Exited, HV_Enabled/Disabled, AlarmSet/Cleared, and
PMDue_Source/Beamline. These events alert the host to configuration changes and required maintenance actions.
Refer to the companion Variable Tables workbook, Sheet 'Collection Events', for the complete list of CEIDs, linked
variables, and trigger conditions.hh	uhNh(hhhh Nub$5fef30ab-7c4e-4efb-bbd6-e60bd672543ah
